We evaluate our approach on forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

title: Error-Based Bidirectional Predictive Coding Enables Deep, 4-Bit Predictive Coding Networks
abstract: Predictive coding networks (PCNs) promise properties not offered by backpropagation-trained networks: learning from purely local information, a single network that both discriminates and generates, and flexible inference by energy minimization. However, their iterative inference is expensive, making hardware acceleration desirable, and a useful, efficient accelerator needs both depth and aggressive quantization. Canonical state-based PC delivers neither: its inference signal decays exponentially with depth, so deep models fail to train, and low precision makes it worse. We show that pairing two recent methods carries the full PCN property set into the deep, 4-bit regime: bidirectional PC (bPC), which unifies discrimination and generation, and the error-based reparameterization (ePC), which optimizes prediction errors rather than states during inference. Error optimization delivers the output signal to every layer in a single backward pass, removing the signal decay; one additional element, global-norm clipping of the error gradients, stabilizes the error dynamics at depth. The resulting ePC+bPC model trains stably up to at least eight layers and retains its full-precision accuracy and clean class-conditional generation under W4A4E4 quantization-aware training, across FP4 and three posit formats. On six-layer networks, where state-based bPC collapses to chance, ePC+bPC classifies more than 50 accuracy points above it after one epoch of training, with class-conditional generations 5-9x better in RMSE. 4-bit quantization is nearly free: full-precision and 4-bit accuracies differ by at most ~5 points, and by under two in the best-performing formats. We characterize the two failure modes the method overcomes, bounded signal decay in state-based PC and error divergence in unregularized error optimization, and discuss implications for a 4-bit-native PCN accelerator.

title: The Anatomy of a Blind Spot: What an LLM Judge Must Be Shown, and How Much
abstract: Evaluation of text generated by large language models (LLMs) is increasingly delegated to LLMs acting as judges, yet what such a judge must be shown remains unresolved. We treat a judge whose reports are acted on as a regulator, in the sense of cybernetics, and ask what it must be shown, how much, in what form, and what its reports must get right. On seven public benchmarks we varied only what the judge was shown. Across three judges whose prices differ 10- to 17-fold, what the judge was shown mattered more than which judge it was. When a system revised its answers on feedback from a judge denied the material they had to respect, it ended below its starting point on instruction following and question answering. On instruction following the loss grew with each round, and it persisted when the judge saw the user's request but not the constraints and with a second judge family. On news summarisation, a correct reference summary beside the source undid most of the source's contribution, whereas on single-answer questions a reference helped. About a tenth of the source did almost all of its work, and a small entailment graph matched an LLM judge at finding errors in grounded text. We committed 83 testable clauses before running; of the 81 that ran, 32 met their bar and 50 went in the predicted direction, and most quantitative predictions from the theory failed. We report every shortfall and derive design rules tied to measured effects.

title: Natural Language Processing for Aligning Readings with Learning Objectives and Assessing Topic Balance in Dental Education
abstract: Curriculum teams often lack time to check whether assigned readings support learning objectives (LOs) and whether topic coverage is balanced. We present a natural language processing (NLP) workflow to support evidence-informed curation of reading lists. The workflow combines PubMedBERT sentence embeddings and cosine similarity for retrieval, natural language inference (NLI) for evidence checking, and topic modeling for coverage analysis. We tested the approach in dental education using 13 course-level LOs and a PubMed-derived corpus of 3,837 LO-abstract pairs. Median cosine similarity ranged from 0.86 to 0.91 across the 13 LOs, showing generally high semantic similarity. Topic modeling showed broad but uneven coverage, with one or two dominant topics per domain. Similarity alone was not enough for selecting readings: among high-similarity pairs (cosine 0.90-1.00), 22.9% were classified by NLI as neutral or contradictory. In a 49-pair expert-labeled validation set, cosine-based retrieval (cosine >= 0.90) achieved 0.69 accuracy, while the combined cosine and NLI approach achieved 0.73 accuracy against expert alignment labels. Overall, the workflow shows how AI can support curriculum alignment by reducing false positives and helping select readings that better match intended LOs.

title: Physics-guided machine learning for saturation control across variable hydraulic conditions in heap leaching
abstract: Heap-leaching hydraulics vary between regions of an ore bed, motivating fast prediction models that accommodate different material properties. This study develops a parameter-conditioned physics-guided machine-learning (PGML) surrogate and demonstrates its use in simulated saturation control. A dataset of 4096 numerical Richards-equation trajectories was divided into 2867 training, 614 validation and 615 evaluation cases. The network predicts hourly saturation profiles from the current profile, irrigation rate and four hydraulic parameters, and is trained with an approximate Gardner mass-balance penalty. A daily predictive controller compared 200 constant irrigation rates over a 24-hour horizon. Across the evaluation cases, the median full-cycle tracking deviation was 4.9% of a 0.70 saturation target, equal to that of a tuned proportional-integral (PI) controller, while the PGML controller reached the target without overshoot in the median and applied approximately 4% less irrigation. Moderate physics guidance reduced long-horizon prediction error by approximately 30% relative to data-only training and reduced irrigation-bound activity, but slightly worsened closed-loop tracking. For a matched prediction workload, the surrogate was approximately 70 times faster than the numerical solver, and batched evaluation cost under 2 ms per column for 5000 columns. The results support a reusable physics-guided surrogate for large-scale saturation control in simulation.

title: Vision: "What Don't I Know About User's Preferences?" How Uncertainty Estimation Improves Proactive Assistant Alignment
abstract: Proactive Smart Assistants (PSAs) increasingly use general knowledge, learned patterns from group-level data, patterns from individual user's data, and recent sensor observations to anticipate which action a user may prefer. Existing systems typically select actions from predicted user preference likelihoods, but these likelihoods alone do not reveal how reliable the prediction is, which evidence supports it, or why ambiguity remains. In this vision paper, we argue that uncertainty estimation can provide this missing information and substantially change appropriate downstream behavior. Using the example of a home assistant, we introduce the questions that uncertainty estimation aims to answer, i.e. how sure is the assistant about the predicted preference likelihood, whether the confidence come from group-level assumptions or individual's data, and whether likelihood ambiguity reflect the user's intrinsic preference variability or insufficient data for the particular situation. We further introduce uncertainty estimation applications in neighboring domains, such as human trajectory prediction, personalized activity recognition, information-collection, and model-based control. Finally, we draw on insights from neighboring domains to envision how future uncertainty-aware proactive assistants may address key challenges in proactive interaction.

title: Hardware-Assisted Multi-Stage Ransomware Detection with Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: Ransomware is a fast-escalating privacy threat causing significant financial and data losses worldwide. As attacks grow more sophisticated, traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to defend. In this paper, we propose an novel framework that couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring to achieve efficient ransomware detection and mitigation. The contributions are threefold: (1) we employ adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation and leverage hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection; (2) we integrate neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalizability; and (3) We validate the proposed approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods. Moreover, it provides trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.

title: Small area learning
abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop standard and cross-fitted estimators for low-complexity and flexible learners, unifying synthetic, model-based, and fully residual-corrected estimation. For area means, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality and provide variance estimators and confidence intervals. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals a bias--variance trade-off: partial residual correction can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to working-model misspecification, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34\%--49\% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. An empirical application favours a cross-fitted estimator using a flexible learner under the chosen validation criterion. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.

title: Instance-Adaptive Online Multiclass Multicalibration
abstract: We study online multiclass multicalibration over $T$ rounds, and give an algorithm with beyond-worst-case guarantees. With $n$ possible outcomes, forecasts lie in a simplex of dimension $d=n-1$. In the worst case, cumulative $\ell_1$ multicalibration error scales with $\widetildeÎ˜(T^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$, which becomes untenable once $d$ exceeds a small constant. Our algorithm adapts to the geometry of the realized sequence: if the sequence of adversarially selected outcome means lies in an affine subspace of dimension $s$, it obtains error $\widetilde O(n^{1/(s+2)}T^{(s+1)/(s+2)})$ with high probability. The algorithm adapts to this structure without knowing the subspace or its dimension. For $T\ge n\ge2$, this rate is minimax optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. For a stochastic instance with a fixed conditional mean, the bound specializes to $\widetilde O(\sqrt{nT})$, giving a square-root dependence on the horizon.

title: Quantum simultaneous decoding via pretty-good measurements of tilted states
abstract: A multiple-access channel transmits messages from several senders to one receiver. For quantum outputs, the receiver must distinguish states depending on all messages, while tests for different decoding errors may not commute. In this paper, we give a self-contained account of simultaneous decoding, in which one joint measurement recovers the messages at the established achievable rates using independent codebooks. The proof combines Sen's tilted-subspace method with Cheng's analysis of the pretty-good measurement, a standard measurement for distinguishing quantum states. Auxiliary labels close to a common reference state separate the geometric directions associated with different errors. A Gram-matrix bound then allows separately chosen binary tests to certify the performance of one measurement. The labels are removed from the completed decoder, leading to a deterministic packing theorem that applies to finite state ensembles, including unequal priors. We develop the two-sender case first, with worked examples and figures, before treating any fixed number of senders. Sharper finite-error guarantees for the same decoder are developed separately, with sharp bounds for two specified steps of the analysis rather than a claim of globally optimal decoding. Applications recover known achievable rates for unassisted and entanglement-assisted classical communication, distributed classical compression with quantum side information, and coherent-state communication through a beamsplitter or passive multiport device. The common proof makes the geometric mechanism and its quantitative consequences available without repeating the construction for each application.

title: ADAPT: Audio-Depth Action Planning with Transition-Aware Rewards for Lights-Out Industrial Navigation
abstract: Vision-language-action models for embodied navigation typically rely on RGB observations, limiting their applicability in lights-out industrial environments where visible illumination may be unavailable. We study illumination-independent navigation using spatial audio for target localization and depth for obstacle-aware geometry. To support this setting, we introduce DarkNav-Bench, a benchmark with 24 industrial scenes and four progressively challenging acoustic conditions. We further propose ADAPT, an audio-depth action-planning framework equipped with spatial-audio perception and optimized for closed-loop navigation through reinforcement learning (RL). Our key RL contribution, transition-aware reward shaping (TARS), defines a pose-aware shortest-action potential over a position-heading graph. Unlike conventional geodesic-progress rewards, TARS accounts for both feasible movements and in-place rotations, providing action-consistent feedback for policy optimization. Experiments show that ADAPT consistently outperforms training-based navigation baselines and zero-shot multimodal models on both seen and unseen scenes. On unseen environments, it achieves 90.6% success under Clean conditions and retains 60.0% success under the most challenging Localized Noise setting. These results demonstrate the potential of spatial audio and depth as complementary modalities for reliable RGB-free navigation in lights-out industrial environments.

title: Harmonic Representations in Symbolic Music Transformers are Localized and Controllable
abstract: Transformer models trained on symbolic music have become remarkably capable. However, it is yet unclear how they represent music structure, and whether understanding their internal representations can be used to unlock methods for model control. We examine this through a case study of harmonic analysis: when a music transformer navigates a cadence, what does it internally "know" about its harmonic context, and can that knowledge be used to affect the generation? Using Aria, a LLaMA-based symbolic music transformer evaluated on Bach chorales, we find that harmonic decisions are causally localized progressively from middle layers onward. Linear probes show that mode becomes decodable in the same layer range where patching identifies growing causal effect, while key identity emerges later. We then confirm these representations are actionable for music generation control: steering via latent directions corresponding to harmonic changes reliably produces a deceptive or minor resolution, while preserving structural coherence and generation quality. This demonstrates that, at inference time, the model's internal harmonic knowledge can be directly manipulated to control the harmonic output.

title: Unfair and Unsafe: Everyday Bias Triggers Emergent Misalignment
abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) occurs when fine-tuning a language model to a narrow task makes it misaligned on unrelated ones. Because organizations now routinely fine-tune models on their own data, it matters which kinds of training data cause EM. So far, studies have induced EM with data containing recognized safety failures, such as insecure code or harmful advice, while biased training data is typically examined by fairness research for the bias models learn from it rather than for its effects on safety. In real-world text, much of this bias, such as demographic stereotypes, appears not as derogatory language but politely, embedded in judgments about people. We ask whether learning such polite stereotypes can itself cause EM. We find that fine-tuning on polite answers that rely on stereotypes makes models less safe and less truthful on unrelated tasks. The effect holds across four open-weight model families (7B to 12B), both gender and race stereotypes, and repeated training runs, relative to controls trained on the same questions without the stereotype. We further show that the learned stereotype has its own direction in model activations, distinct from directions for generic misaligned traits such as deception. This direction exists before fine-tuning and can both control the learned stereotype and monitor its acquisition. Existing defenses against EM improve safety while leaving the stereotype largely intact. Beyond this controlled setting, fine-tuning on political news coverage also triggers EM, apparently amplified by partisan framing, and stereotype models acting as tool-using agents can carry out harmful tasks and blame people without evidence. Our results show that biased training data is not only a fairness problem but also a safety one. We argue that EM is studied too narrowly, and that fairness concerns and methods offer a natural way to broaden the search for its triggers.

title: Using Line Segment Tracking to enable ML-based Track Reconstruction in CMS
abstract: High-pileup conditions in CMS during the HL-LHC era make charged-particle tracking increasingly challenging as detector occupancy and combinatorics grow. We present a hybrid approach that exploits Line Segment Tracking (LST) objects rather than individual hits to enable the first CMS ML-based track reconstruction algorithm. The LST objects, namely the triplets used in this study, are built according to geometry- and physics-driven criteria and carry richer local structure, geometrical cues, and physics quantities such as transverse momentum, which helps the model incorporate detector-level information from the start. We apply a Transformer encoder with geometrically masked sparse self-attention to embed these objects in a learned latent space, and use object condensation to assemble full tracks in a single inference step. This object-based representation reduces complexity in dense environments and makes the model less sensitive to ambiguities introduced by high pileup. Evaluated on CMS Phase-2 simulation of $t\bar{t}$ events at $\langle Î¼\rangle = 200$, the approach achieves reconstruction efficiency comparable to the LST quintuplet baseline while reducing the fake rate by roughly a factor of three and suppressing duplicates almost entirely, demonstrating the promise of advanced ML architectures for next-generation particle tracking.

title: Small but Mighty: Test Suites as Improvement Signals for Self-Evolving Agents
abstract: A self-evolving agent rewrites its own harness and must decide which rewrites to keep, so its improvement signal is the check a rewrite has to pass. Verifying a rewrite by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, while executable checks such as the repository's own tests are too sparse to catch behavior-changing rewrites, rejecting only a quarter of them. We instead take test feedback as the executable signal, and search for test suites that are both small and strong with a quality-diversity evolutionary algorithm, so that the signal is dense and informative. TeSearch treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so that quality is pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on that descriptor. Across 129 real-world modules and three backbones, TeSearch delivers the highest-quality suites of any method compared, LLM-driven evolutionary search included, and the smallest of any LLM-based one. Used as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent, it rejects 59.9% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3% for the repository's tests, at a 4.0% false-alarm rate and 3.5 s per decision. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/TeSearch.

title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs
abstract: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. In particular, optimizing batch size together with epoch counts reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size, favoring smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization. We further find that training recipes, previously optimized under a single-pass assumption, can be tuned, e.g., repacking documents into new sequences every epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay. We then relax the infinite-compute assumption. In particular, smaller-than-typical batch sizes can require prohibitively long sequential training, motivating to treat GPUs and time as separate resources. Tighter deadlines favor larger batches, and latency-oriented parallelism can trade additional GPUs for shorter training. Nevertheless, even under a fixed time budget, a smaller batch with fewer GPUs can achieve lower validation loss than a larger batch with more GPUs, challenging the common practice of increasing data parallelism to maximize GPU utilization under a deadline. Together, our results identify underexplored factors in repeated-data training and provide concrete guidance on how training recipes and resource allocation should change from single-pass pretraining.

title: Softmax-Free Attention in Spiking Transformers as the Zero-Temperature Limit of Two-Level Systems
abstract: Spiking Transformers achieve energy efficiency by discarding softmax normalization in favor of thresholded, binary attention. However, this removal breaks the thermodynamic framework used to analyze attention networks, as the normalized measure and partition function cease to exist. We restore this theoretical foundation by proving that softmax-free spiking attention operates exactly as the zero-temperature limit of a product of independent two-level systems. This correspondence places spiking attention strictly in the frozen ordered phase of the thermodynamic phase diagram for all inputs. Consequently, the entropic cost of organizing attention collapses, replaced by a Landauer-type physical floor governed by action-potential generation. Furthermore, this ordered-phase pinning mathematically explains the optimization difficulty caused by vanishing surrogate gradients. We validate this theory with forward-relaxation experiments, placing both standard and neuromorphic attention mechanisms on a unified thermodynamic axis.

title: PopGen: Generating Semantically Diverse Populations for Zero-Shot Coordination
abstract: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, exposing a cooperator to partners with diverse strategies during training is key to better collaboration at test time. However, existing methods typically rely on trajectory-level proxies to measure diversity, which may label two distinct trajectories of the same strategy as diverse. Instead, our key insight is to leverage LLMs' ability to describe behaviorally distinct agents in environments, similar to how humans can recognize high-level strategies. To this end, we introduce PopGen, a framework that synthesizes semantically diverse agents from scratch using LLMs. PopGen first generates a diverse set of textual descriptions of agent behaviors, then translates each behavior into a code policy that can be executed within the environment. We show that cooperators trained against PopGen populations achieve robust zero-shot cooperation with unseen partners, outperforming population-play baselines across four collaborative environments. We further show that semantic diversity scales with PopGen population size, improving the cooperator's worst-case performance, and we identify design choices that preserve population quality while maximizing diversity. Our code is available at https://github.com/labicon/PopGen.

title: Probing black holes extremality bounds with non-extensive entropies
abstract: Due to the importance of studying quantum-gravity-induced corrections to Einstein's theory of gravity, it is of interest to consider non-extensive entropies whose potential applications include identifying such corrections. In this Letter, we investigate possible corrections to a universal relation associated with the extremality bound of the mass of a black hole by employing entropies defined as functions of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy.

title: Scalable Exact Non-Pauli Noise Simulation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum design relies on simulating noisy quantum error correction (QEC) circuits with hundreds to thousands of physical qubits and large circuit depths. High-throughput stabilizer simulators, such as Stim, are the de facto tools for this regime. However, these simulators typically support only Clifford gates and stochastic Pauli noise. As a result, more realistic device noise models-such as coherent control errors and thermal relaxation-are often approximated using Pauli Twirling. This replacement offers speed but can introduce inaccuracies. To address this, we propose QuasiStim for scalable exact QEC simulation of realistic noise, with QuasiFold as a compiler frontend and DeltaFrame as a sampling backend. QuasiFold lowers sampling overhead by merging equivalent non-Pauli sites in the quantum circuit. DeltaFrame samples the resulting stabilizer trajectories by reusing precomputed predicted references instead of resimulating the full tableau for each shot. QuasiFold can reduce the number of shots by over $100\times$ on bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes. Compared to a per-shot tableau simulator, DeltaFrame is $166\times$--$1331\times$ faster on rotated surface-code memory under coherent $R_Z$ noise as $d$ grows from 5 to 35. QuasiStim also makes the PTA bias measurable: the gap is non-negligible and varies with noise strength, decoder, and circuit schedule. QuasiStim will be open-sourced upon publication at https://github.com/isaachyw/QuasiStim

title: Embedding Information in Policy Randomness: Distribution-Preserving Implicit Communication in MDPs
abstract: This paper investigates a new role of randomness in stochastic policies--as a medium for embedding and communicating information. Specifically, we consider an agent interacting with an environment according to a prescribed stochastic policy. By carefully modulating the random action realizations of the policy, information can be embedded into the agent's behavior without altering the prescribed action distribution. We cast this problem as a channel coding problem, in which the controlled system implicitly serves as a communication channel. We then propose a coding scheme, termed posterior-matching randomness modulation (PRAM), that selects actions according to the message to be transmitted. With the aid of common randomness independent of the control system, PRAM preserves the prescribed action distribution for every state and every message. We further prove that PRAM is asymptotically reliable: the message can be decoded with arbitrarily small error probability as the observed state trajectory becomes sufficiently long. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in applications including multi-bit policy watermarking and trajectory provenance.

title: Mixed Feelings, Single Polarity
abstract: Emotion datasets are routinely mapped onto positive and negative valence, by assigning each emotion category one polarity. We test where this works and where it fails, using SemEval-2018 Affect in Tweets (English, Arabic, Spanish), Affective Text aligned with EmoBank, raw GoEmotions annotations, naturalistic hashtag corpora, and a controlled annotation study. Fixed projection works well when a text carries labels of one valence. It fails on a subset identifiable from the labels alone: tweets whose emotion labels point in opposite directions. These are 9.0% of polar SemEval test tweets but cause 54.8% of the polarity errors of a learned projection, are more than twice as likely to receive a neutral-or-mixed gold label, and are not rescued by modeling the full label set. Annotators produce such configurations routinely: 16.3% of multilabel GoEmotions judgments combine emotions from the dataset's own positive and negative parents. In a controlled study holding word and reader constant, context changes the coarse valence judgment in 56.8% of cases, against 19.9% for controls. We recommend projecting label configurations rather than labels, abstaining or keeping a mixed class where labels conflict, and reporting coverage alongside accuracy.

title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Wildfire Size Using Conditional Flow Matching
abstract: In this work we present a probabilistic model for predicting the temporal evolution of wildfire size using conditional generative algorithms, namely flow matching. Rather than predicting spatially resolved fire progression, the proposed model forecasts a time series of fire acreage, substantially reducing computational cost and enabling efficient integration with downstream applications such as early warning systems and risk assessment tools. Given estimates of the fire size at the current and previous forecasting steps, alongside spatially averaged weather conditions, terrain characteristics, and fuel composition, the model predicts the change in fire area over a 3-hour interval. Training data are drawn from 140 coupled atmosphere-wildfire simulations generated using WRF-SFIRE, paired with weather data from the North American Mesoscale (NAM) model. Sensitivity analysis demonstrates that the model captures physically-consistent responses to variations in wind speed, temperature, and relative humidity. Model performance is evaluated against reference solutions from WRF-SFIRE. For single-step predictions, the model achieves a symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE) of 0.39 relative to the reference WRF-SFIRE solutions. Recursive multi-step predictions over 24 hours are performed for 12 held-out test cases, where the flow matching model achieves a final fire area sMAPE of 0.39 while further providing meaningful quantification of forecast uncertainty.

title: Symmetric Dual Breather Modes as a Dynamic Origin of Tiny Particle Masses
abstract: Spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) is conventionally understood through static vacuum selection in low-energy approximations. However, the nonperturbative dynamical pathways connecting symmetric configurations to asymmetric states remain an open question. In this paper, we propose an operator-theoretic framework that characterizes $Z_{2}$ symmetry breaking in scalar field theory through spectral branching. Specifically, we identify an effective invariant manifold of the nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation termed the "symmetric dual breather mode," whose phase-space geometry is traced using a $t$-dependent finite-dimensional representation. Our analysis demonstrates that static SSB represents merely a small-amplitude limit ($A \ll Ï†_{v1}$). As the amplitude increases into the heteroclinic regime ($A > Ï†_{v1}$), the field dynamically overflows the central barrier, yielding a vanishing time-averaged order parameter ($\langle Ï†\rangle = 0$) and driving a geometric curvature cancellation ($\langle V''(Ï†) \rangle_{t} \to 0$). Governed by a universal scaling function $\mathfrak{F}(y)$, the logarithmic period divergence near the heteroclinic boundary naturally generates sub-eV effective mass scales without fine-tuning bare parameters. Furthermore, this dynamic barrier overflow naturally favors Majorana-like self-conjugate states over Dirac-type states. Additionally, nonlinear phase interference along the heteroclinic channel induces asymmetric phase-space contraction, decoupling the right-handed mode and dynamically giving rise to the left-handed Weyl equation. These results bridge nonperturbative wave dynamics, topological mass suppression, chiral selection, and the dynamic origin of active neutrino masses.

title: Revocation Is Not Complete at Receipt: An Executable Outcome Contract for Distributed Agent-Tool Gateways
abstract: Distributed agent workflows cache delegated authority at tool gateways. Revocation may be reported at issuer commit, transport acknowledgment, or receiver persistence, although none of these observations establishes that all gateways enforced the change or that guarded effects stopped. We define C0-C5, a bounded outcome contract spanning issuer commit through effect prevention, and implement it as a persistent monitor over a frozen gateway set, call set, and observation window. A 14-case fault matrix checks conservative classification, sticky violations, restart persistence, and evidence immutability. In a derived audit of its eight semantic cases, treating C3 or C4 as completion produces seven or five false positives, respectively; the bounded C0-C5 verdict produces none. Descriptive scaling covers 1,024 gateways and 10,000 effect vectors. The primary experiment uses the maintained Keycloak 26.7 identity server and measures the contract across two durable receivers, eight physical agent-tool gateways, Filesystem and PostgreSQL effects, and 16 AWS hosts in three availability zones. Normal delivery and recovery commit no effects. Under receiver-selective non-delivery, transport acknowledgment and receiver persistence still succeed, but 112 of 225 calls (49.78%) are admitted, and all 112 effects commit in every treatment block. A separately provisioned execution repeats the result. OPA/Toxiproxy and a live three-role LLM workflow with networked MCP tools reproduce the persisted-but-not-enforced boundary on narrower surfaces. Finally, an unmodified external MCPMark agent executes 60 closed-loop task arms. Normal C4 denies all 31 exposed post-barrier calls and commits no effect; selective C3 allows 344 calls and commits 145 effects across Filesystem and PostgreSQL. Transport success is therefore evidence of progress, not a revocation-completion verdict.

title: Handoff Curves: Initial Selection, Later Handoff, and Supervision Targets in Multi-turn LLM Routing
abstract: We study how initial model selection, later handoff, and training targets affect success and cost in LLM tasks that span multiple turns. We compare several router architectures using handoff curves, which record task success and cost as the handoff step changes. Our dataset contains 34,204 complete executions of three Qwen models across BFCL, MultiWOZ, and $Ï„$-retail, providing offline supervision for routing decisions. In our primary comparison, with Qwen3.5 35B-A3B as the starting model, allowing a later handoff does not establish an improvement in utility over initial selection on BFCL or MultiWOZ, and increases cost on BFCL across a range of cost weights. Changing the supervision targets improves router performance on both our dataset and TwinRouterBench. On our dataset, replacing noisy training success curves with monotone fits raises success by 0.2 to 4.1 percentage points at the same cost across the reported operating points. On TwinRouterBench, we construct targets that describe the model capability needed for the remaining work and difficult steps ahead. Compared with training on the benchmark's per-step labels, these targets raise trajectory pass scores by 7.8 percentage points and cost savings by 6.3 percentage points on the full static bank. A live deployment of the router trained with these targets resolves 79 of 100 instances at a router cost of 0.59 US dollars per instance.

title: Large language model-generated patterns for epidemiological modeling: a multi-benchmark evaluation framework
abstract: Representing individual-level behavioral heterogeneity is challenging in epidemiological modeling, particularly when empirical behavioral data are sparse. We assess the potential of large language model (LLM)-generated behavioral outputs in addressing this challenge, using hepatitis C virus-related behaviors among people who inject drugs as a case study. Correspondence with epidemiological patterns was evaluated using external benchmarks: literature-informed association directions, correlations from an agent-based model (ABM), and survey associations. Across three LLMs, unconditional directional recovery across 28 retained literature-informed associations was 46-68%, compared with 82-93% agreement when LLMs were directly asked to classify the same associations. Mean absolute differences from ABM and survey correlation patterns were 0.11-0.13 and 0.15-0.18, respectively. Together, these findings show partial alignment between LLM-generated behavioral relationships and epidemiological evidence, despite higher knowledge-probe agreement. More systematic evaluation is needed before incorporating LLM-generated behavioral outputs into epidemiological models that simulate transmission dynamics.

title: AutoSec-RAN: Specification-Grounded LLM Fine-Tuning for Automated Security Analysis of O-RAN
abstract: This paper presents AutoSec-RAN, a specification-grounded large language model (LLM) framework for automated security triage of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) testing. Unlike approaches relying on static rule sets or privileged access to raw packet captures, AutoSec-RAN fine-tunes Mistral-7B-Instruct through two Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) stages over a curated corpus of 69 O-RAN, 3GPP, and adjacent standards documents, then selectively augments inference with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the same specification index. At inference, the model receives only an investigator-style question and a scenario metadata block, simulating an automated analyst operating without raw packet evidence. AutoSec-RAN is validated on a purpose-built 5G/O-RAN testbed across labeled fronthaul distributed denial of service replay scenarios. A Gemma-4-31B judge LLM scores each candidate's answer on faithfulness, correctness, and actionability relative to a reference authored from full packet capture and log evidence. AutoSec-RAN achieves a mean judge overall score of 0.713 across all 313 evaluation items (0.755 restricted to the five supervised taxonomy classes), clearing the 0.70 reporting threshold, and a blended score of 0.778 (0.808 supervised-only) when cosine similarity over Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) General Embedding (BGE) is incorporated as a secondary semantic signal. The framework performs strongest on mitigation and threat-model reasoning (with a mean overall of 0.849 and 0.848, respectively) and identifies a measurable gap on the held-out attack-direction class (0.515), a controlled result that exposes a specific training data requirement. These results establish specification-grounded LoRA fine-tuning combined with RAG retrieval as a viable foundation for automated security validation of AI-native O-RAN.

title: Dissipative Lagrangian Neural Networks for the Interpretable Modelling of Passive Mechanical Systems
abstract: In this paper, we propose the Dissipative Lagrangian Neural Network (dLNN), a continuous-time system identification technique that separately learns the conservative and dissipative dynamics of a mechanical system directly from data. A key contribution is a novel parametrisation of dissipative forces that (i) is structurally constrained to be dissipative, enforcing passivity of the learned model, (ii) cannot absorb conservative mechanics, and (iii) retains sufficient expressivity to represent a broad family of state-dependent damping and regularised friction forces. The model is validated on prediction tasks on two real-world mechanical systems: trajectory prediction of a chaotic double pendulum and inverse-dynamics modelling of a six-degree-of-freedom industrial robot. Across these tasks, the dLNN demonstrates improved predictive performance over existing Lagrangian architectures while remaining competitive with a black-box neural model. The imposed physical structure also improves generalisation to unseen states, with the benefits becoming particularly pronounced when training data is limited. Finally, we introduce a symbolic distillation procedure that extracts closed-form expressions from the learned physical components. Applied to the industrial robot, this produces interpretable symbolic models that retain high predictive accuracy while reducing the computational overhead associated with evaluating neural Lagrangian models.

title: Representational Difference Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers representational knowledge from a large teacher network to a compact student. Existing relational and contrastive distillation methods treat all samples uniformly, spending equal gradient on well-matched and poorly-matched regions of the representation space alike. We propose Representational Difference Distillation (RDD), which diagnoses where teacher and student representations structurally disagree and concentrates the distillation signal on those regions. RDD uses two asymmetric affinity matrices that capture opposing directions of misalignment: one identifies samples the student incorrectly considers similar, the other identifies teacher relationships the student has yet to learn. These affinities determine which sample pairs the distillation loss aligns and how strongly it corrects each misaligned sample. On CIFAR-100 with resnet32x4 to resnet8x4, RDD reaches 75.58% test accuracy in our runs, on par with CRD (75.45%) and above KD and RKD. We additionally explore curriculum-based and sampling-based variants, finding that weighting the loss is more effective than filtering the data.

title: A 4-Qubit Variational Quantum Classifier for Sequence-Specific Classification of DNMT3A and DNMT3B Flanking Methylation Preferences
abstract: DNA methylation is a critical epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression and genome stability, primarily catalyzed by the DNA methyltransferase 3 (DNMT3) family of enzymes. Distinguishing precise sequence-specific flanking preferences between DNMT3A and DNMT3B remains computationally challenging due to the complex and high-dimensional nature of biochemical sequence data. In this study, we propose a novel Quantum Machine Learning (QML) approach to classify DNA methylation preferences, leveraging a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC). Using experimentally derived deep enzymology data, we constructed a dataset containing 4,096 unique NNNCGNNN motifs. We evaluated a four-qubit VQC using a custom NumPy exact-statevector simulator. The described two-layer circuit contains 24 trainable rotations, eight CNOT gates, and eight input-encoding rotations, totaling 40 gates before measurement. Across five initialization seeds, the revised VQC evaluation achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.661 pm 0.009, where variability denotes sample standard deviation. The held-out test partition is approximately balanced, containing 200 DNMT3A-labeled motifs and 210 DNMT3B-labeled motifs. An always-DNMT3B predictor achieves 51.2% accuracy and a balanced accuracy of 0.500 on this test partition. This proof-of-concept establishes a foundation for utilizing near-term quantum architectures in complex epigenetic classification tasks, paving the way for hybrid quantum-classical pipelines in bioinformatics.

title: PAIR: Memory-Efficient and Fast Inference with Reading--Reasoning Fusion
abstract: For context-based question answering, using one large model for both evidence extraction and answer reasoning requires substantial memory and computation. Existing approaches trade accuracy for efficiency within a single model only. We propose a multi-model approach for efficient inference: our method, PAIR, employs two differently sized models for evidence extraction and answer reasoning, respectively. A smaller Reader model processes and retains the full context, while a larger Reasoner model sees only the question and generated sequence without directly attending to the context. These capabilities are fused at the logit level: at each token, both Reader and Reasoner produce a prediction, and their logits are combined into one, behaving as a single next-token-prediction model. Fine-tuning further boosts their performance. On HotpotQA, PAIR with a 32B Reasoner retains 96% of that same 32B model's full-context accuracy while using roughly one quarter of its KV memory. At 45.7K-token contexts, PAIR achieves up to 3.2$\times$ higher end-to-end throughput than the full-context 32B model on the same GPU. PAIR also improves the accuracy-memory and accuracy-throughput trade-offs over evaluated token-reduction baselines. Its accuracy-preserving behavior generalizes across Qwen2.5, OLMo-3, and Gemma-3 model families.

title: Improving the Evaluation of Biomedical Question Answering with Few Human Preference Signals
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly used for biomedical Question Answering (QA). However, evaluating their effectiveness remains challenging due to the lack of reliable reference resources and the frequent misalignment between automatic evaluation metrics and human judgments. One practical question is how evaluation results should be used to guide development decisions, especially when they correlate weakly with human judgments and may even lead to different conclusions. We explore how to use a small amount of human preference signals to calibrate direct assessment evaluation metrics, and show that calibrated metrics consistently outperform baselines that either treat all metrics equally or rely on a single best metric across multiple datasets.

title: Meaningful Moments: A Corpus of VLM-Derived Temporal Importance Labels for Video Action Recognition
abstract: Not every moment in a video is equally useful for recognizing an action. A few decisive moments often carry the evidence: the instant an object moves, the peak of a dive, or one object placed on another. Existing video datasets rarely provide large-scale, action-conditioned labels for which short segments carry that evidence. This work asks whether vision-language models can identify meaningful moments at scale and whether those labels improve action recognition. We introduce Meaningful Moments (MM), a corpus of about 4.58 million VLM-generated per-segment importance scores for nearly 500,000 class-labeled videos spanning Something-Something v2 (SSv2), Kinetics-400 (K400), and Diving-48 across 622 action classes. We freeze the action classifier and vary only temporal sampling. An alpha-parameterized comparison of importance-led selection against an importance-inverted control separates gains from the VLM signal from gains caused by variable-density sampling alone. Across all three datasets, VLM-derived importance is informative: at the hard-cut endpoint, keeping VLM-important segments outperforms keeping VLM-designated filler. Usefulness depends on class structure. On Diving-48, importance-led fast-forwarding preserves full-video recognition while the inverted control collapses by roughly 30 percentage points. On K400, hard-cut selection beats uniform sampling by 1.45 percentage points, rising to 2.05 under threshold selection. On SSv2, the labels carry signal but do not recover full-video performance. Direct scoring matches greedy removal within its noise floor at roughly 25 times fewer oracle calls, and a four-VLM cross-oracle study shows consistent downstream trends. We release the importance labels and evaluation protocol under CC-BY-4.0; SSv2 class strings remain under CC-BY-NC-4.0.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Camera-Radar Sensor Fusion for Autonomous Driving
abstract: Autonomous driving (AD) relies on multi-sensor perception to interpret the surrounding environment. However, the robustness of camera--radar fusion under adversarial conditions remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a systematic measurement study of the robustness of camera--radar sensor fusion in AD. We construct a unified evaluation pipeline on the nuScenes dataset that simulates attacks on both sensing modalities, including eight camera-image perturbations and three radar point-cloud perturbations. We evaluate five camera--radar fusion algorithms across two perception tasks, 3D object detection and depth estimation, and quantify their performance under clean and attacked inputs using standard metrics. Our evaluation reveals a clear asymmetry in the robustness of fusion systems. Camera perturbations substantially degrade both object detection and depth estimation, and moderate attack strengths are already sufficient to cause severe performance degradation. In contrast, the evaluated radar perturbations produce smaller and task-dependent effects, with object-detection models showing particularly limited degradation. Our analysis attributes this difference to the strong dependence of existing fusion architectures on dense camera features, together with the filtering, association, and confidence-weighting mechanisms commonly applied to sparse radar measurements. These results demonstrate that sensor fusion does not inherently guarantee robustness and that the contribution and reliability of each sensing modality must be explicitly considered under adversarial conditions. Based on four empirical findings, we derive measurement-guided design implications for future robust camera--radar fusion, including modality-specific reliability estimation, cross-modal consistency checking, adaptive fusion, and graceful failover under severe sensor degradation.

title: Computational Reflective Equilibrium for Agentic AI: A Rawlsian Alignment Scaffold for Governance
abstract: The rapid deployment of agentic AI has introduced complex challenges for the ethics and governance of AI systems. Agents built on large language models act through tools on behalf of people, and each deployment case brings its own instructions, policies, evidence, and stakeholders, so alignment must be formed case by case. To this end, this work proposes agentic reflective equilibrium (ARE), a computational reflective equilibrium framework that serves as an ethical alignment scaffold in the agent harness. Drawing inspiration from the reflective equilibrium of John Rawls, the scaffold links principles from the system prompt and operator policy, considered judgments, tool evidence, and candidate actions through typed support and attack relations, with provenance encoding the instruction hierarchy. The agent acts on an equilibrium of this state and calls tools or asks questions only while doing so is worth its cost, unless a due-diligence mandate requires them. Governance enters through value priorities, source authority, prohibitions, human-in-the-loop triggers, and mandates, and certificates attribute each action to the sources whose commitments drove it. We show that equilibria are Nash equilibria of a mutual-adjustment game and establish monotonicity, lexical priority, stability certificates, and a quarantine theorem for prompt injection. Two case studies illustrate the framework: a computer-use assistant told to win a refund "whatever it takes" files an honest warranty claim, refuses a fake review, and ignores an injected request for personal data; a hiring agent showcases how authority, oversight triggers, audit mandates, and hard prohibitions shape discrimination, privacy violations, and escalation. The framework offers traceability, coherence, and adaptivity, facilitating safe, secure, and trustworthy agentic AI.

title: Certified Robustness via Sparse Second-Order Cone Relaxations
abstract: Certified robustness is critical for deploying neural networks in safety-sensitive settings, but computing exact certificates typically requires solving nonconvex optimization problems. Practical verifiers use convex relaxations: linear programming (LP) relaxations are scalable but often too conservative, whereas semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations can be substantially tighter but are computationally expensive. We introduce a hierarchy of second-order cone programming (SOCP) relaxations that provide stronger certificates than LP while avoiding the cost of global positive-semidefinite constraints. Our construction combines convex-hull relaxations of ReLU activations, selective McCormick lifting over certified variable bounds, and second-order cone constraints induced by 2-by-2 principal minors. Adding these constraints progressively yields a monotone hierarchy of increasingly tight bounds with a controllable computation-tightness trade-off. On fully connected and convolutional networks on MNIST and CIFAR-10, SOCP-based verification improves certified robust accuracy over LP-based verification and is competitive with alpha,beta-CROWN, while remaining orders of magnitude faster than SDP-based verification. These results position selective second-order constraints as a practical middle ground between scalable LP-based and tight SDP-based certification. Finally, we introduce class-optimized robust evaluation (CORE), which applies tighter relaxations only to target classes not certified by cheaper ones. On the fully connected MNIST benchmark, CORE variants match SDP-cert's certified robust accuracy while reducing average verification time by up to 86.30%.

title: Adaptive Entanglement Witnessing for Two-Qubit Systems
abstract: Entanglement witnesses are a key instrument in determining the entanglement of unknown bipartite qubit systems without requiring a full tomography. Riccardi et al. (2020) proposed a set of two-qubit witnesses, denoted $\{W^3\}$, which require a set of local measurements in three bases. In this work we propose an additional set of witnesses, denoted $\{W^5\}$, that build on $\{W^3\}$ and require measurements in two additional bases. We present an adaptive two-step method that uses the measurement results obtained for $\{W^3\}$ to select which $W^5$ to evaluate. We computationally demonstrate that our adaptive two-step protocol can identify 72% of entangled states generated according to the methods of Roik et al. (2021) while requiring measurements in only five of the nine bases needed for full quantum tomography. Additionally, we experimentally verify the behavior of both sets of witnesses using polarization-entangled photon pairs.

title: When Does Compensating Inherited Quantization Error Help? Mean-Square Guarantees for Layer-Wise Quantization and Their Limits
abstract: Layer-wise post-training quantization methods let each layer compensate for the quantization error inherited from earlier layers. We ask under what assumptions such compensation guarantees a network output error no larger than without it. For linear networks of any depth, with the required calibration Gram matrices invertible, if the rounding error of each layer has zero conditional mean and a deterministic second-moment map common to both schemes, as under subtractive dither on an unbounded grid, then compensation with strengths in $[0,1]$ fixed in advance gives a mean-square output error no larger than no compensation, each scheme being followed along its own trajectory. The exact gain separates error removed directly from reduced excitation of later rounding noise. Outside this setting the comparison can fail. With rectified linear activations it fails for two independent reasons: noise changes activation states, and, even when no state changes, the correction moves error from samples on which a unit is inactive to samples on which it is active. With stable activations, commutators between the calibration projection and the activation patterns bound the excess. With a bounded codebook, even unique exact layer-wise minimizers with no overload can give a larger output error. For fixed rounding errors it already fails for two scalar linear layers, refuting a published universal guarantee. An exact residual identity gives the necessary and sufficient condition on a common layer input. All these comparisons hold the calibration input fixed. On two 8B models at 4 bits, fixed half-strength compensation beat uncompensated rounding in every model, text and draw tested, yet no rule for choosing the strength beat a layer-wise rule consistently, and lowering the full-network loss on the data used to choose did not reliably lower it on new text.

title: Removing the Compute Bottleneck for Event-based Visual Place Recognition with Spiking Neural Networks
abstract: Neuromorphic sensing and computing promise low latency and high energy efficiency for robotics, yet most event-based visual place recognition (VPR) pipelines reintroduce dense, frame-like computation downstream of an inherently sparse sensor, forfeiting the sensor's latency advantage. In this paper, we address the problem of resolving an event-based VPR query in tens of microseconds on a commodity CPU. We train a two-layer spiking neural network (SNN) with additive spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), which drives the learned weight matrix towards a strongly bimodal distribution, amenable to aggressive magnitude pruning. At inference, our pipeline exploits this sparsity by reading only the pruned weights corresponding to the query's active pixels. As surviving weights share a near-uniform magnitude, each neuron's score reduces to an integer count of matching synapses instead of a weighted sum, lowering per-query latency. This computation is small enough to remain resident in a CPU's fast on-chip cache. On three event-based VPR benchmarks, our sparse SNN exceeds the recall of LENS, an existing event-based SNN, while reducing per-query latency by 5.5-6.2x to tens of microseconds. It matches the recall of a dense variant of our network and of the sum-of-absolute-differences (SAD) baseline, while reading 10x fewer weights than the dense variant. We further characterise how recall and latency scale with the number of active pixels and reference places. These results suggest that the sparsity of both event-based input and learned weights can already be exploited for low-latency inference on conventional processors.

title: Of Errors and Echoes: Responsibility-Aware Credit Assignment for Tool-Use Agents
abstract: Reinforcement learning improves tool-use agents, yet fine-grained credit assignment remains challenging even with step-level feedback. An observed error may be inherited from an earlier decision, while multiple responsible decisions may share the same downstream consequence or participate in later recovery. We introduce Error-Chain-Aware Optimization (ECHO), a responsibility-aware credit assignment framework that separates responsibility identification from credit allocation. A frozen judge combines retrospective trajectory analysis with decision-time assessment from the policy-visible prefix to distinguish newly introduced errors, inherited consequences, missed corrections, and successful corrections. ECHO then counts shared downstream consequences once across responsible decisions and constrains rewards for repairing self-induced errors through source-funded recovery, producing bounded action-level supervision alongside terminal supervision. Experiments on six diverse tool-use benchmarks at both 4B and 8B scales show strong and consistent improvements over the compared baselines, with ECHO achieving the highest score on five of six benchmarks at each scale. These results support decision responsibility as a useful basis for fine-grained credit assignment in tool-use agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/xid32/ECHO.

title: Limit Theory for Online Expectile Estimation under Short and Long Range Dependence
abstract: Expectiles are tail-sensitive distributional summaries with important applications in financial risk measurement and forecasting, yet statistical theory for their online estimation from dependent data remains limited. We study a one-pass, stochastic-gradient algorithm with constant learning rate $Î³$ for estimating the marginal expectile of a stationary causal process. The recursion admits a unique stationary causal solution and geometrically forgets its initialization. Under short-range dependence, its last iterate is asymptotically Gaussian at the $\sqrtÎ³$ scale, with variance governed by the population curvature and the long-run variance of the expectile score. For long-memory linear processes the scale changes to $Î³^{Î²-1/2}\ell(1/Î³)$, with a Gaussian limit arising from a fractional Brownian motion integral. We further derive the joint long-memory limit for multiple expectile levels and characterize its limiting covariance structure. Various numerical experiments corroborate the predicted Gaussian approximations and regime-specific fluctuation scales.

title: Sequential optimization for orbital-optimized variational quantum eigensolvers
abstract: Orbital optimization within the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) framework is useful for improving active-space quality and accurately capturing electron correlation with shallow quantum circuits. The orbital-optimized unitary coupled cluster (OO-UCC) method [W. Mizukami et al., Phys. Rev. Res. 2, 033421 (2020)], in its original formulation, employs the orbital gradient and Hessian in a Newton--Laphson procedure. In this study, we propose sequential orbital-optimized unitary coupled cluster doubles (SOO-UCCD), extending the gradient-free sequential minimal optimization approach [K. M. Nakanishi et al., Phys. Rev. Res. 2, 043158 (2020)] to orbital rotation parameters. Based on the frequency structure implied by the algebraic properties of the orbital rotation generators, our method determines each orbital rotation angle from a nine-point energy profile. The energy landscape is evaluated by classically transforming the Hamiltonian integrals and contracting them with the reduced density matrices already measured for the VQE energy evaluation. This allows for orbital optimization without evaluating the orbital gradient or Hessian. By building on the core benefits of the OO-UCC framework, our method provides a gradient-free and hyperparameter-free orbital-optimization procedure. State-vector simulations for LiH in the STO-3G basis show that SOO-UCCD reproduces UCCSD-level accuracy along the bond-stretching curve and exhibits macro-iteration convergence comparable to that of L-BFGS-based orbital optimization.

title: A Nonlinear Time-Series Theory for Constant-step SGD with Momentum
abstract: Constant-step stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGDM) augments the parameter recursion with a momentum state that carries geometrically decaying memory of past stochastic gradients. We study this coupled recursion as a nonlinear time series and develop a framework for its stationary behavior and distributional limits. The joint parameter-momentum process forgets its initialization geometrically under a finite $p$th moment for $p > 1$, yielding a unique stationary causal solution. Under a second-moment condition, this contraction leads to an invariance principle and quenched Gaussian limit for averaged SGDM, while a small-learning-rate analysis gives a Gaussian limit for the last iterate. In a stochastic-curvature quadratic model, we further study how the rate of initialization forgetting relates to stationary variance and averaged fluctuations.

title: OT-FlowRec: Optimal Transport-Guided Multi-Bridge Flow for Multimodal Sequential Recommendation
abstract: E-commerce user preferences evolve dynamically within sessions, exhibiting concurrent and multi-centric interest distributions. While existing multimodal sequential recommendation methods leverage global attention to compress historical interactions, they inadequately capture the concurrent nature of multi-interest behaviors and fail to model the underlying multi-centric distribution of user intent. To tackle this issue, we propose OT-FlowRec, an optimal transport-guided multi-bridge flow matching framework that explicitly models multi-interest distributions to facilitate multimodal sequential recommendation. Unlike single-path generative models, OT-FlowRec constructs a mixture of parallel, interest-specific transport flows to model the multi-centric distribution characteristics, where each flow preserves a distinct user interest cluster via an optimal transport plan. Then, a geometric transport mechanism is designed to establish minimum-cost paths from the latent multi-interest distribution to target preference prototypes to provide multi-interest awareness. Moreover, a progressive time-sampling warmup strategy dynamically biases optimization weights toward the final states of the generation process, bridging the gap between continuous global distribution fitting and practical top-$k$ ranking metrics. This approach achieves explicit interest disentanglement, ensuring the preservation of a multi-peaked preference representation instead of collapsing it into a unimodal average. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that OT-FlowRec outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.

title: When Agents Talk, Secrets Travel: Topology-Driven Leakage and Recipient-Conditioned Sanitization in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems (MALS) introduce a privacy-leakage problem that conventional sensitivity-based defenses miss, since information disclosed to one authorized agent can propagate through routine coordination to an unauthorized one, without compromise or malicious behavior. This motivates topology-aware enforcement that blocks unauthorized propagation while preserving authorized disclosure. We evaluate 485 scenarios across coordinator-worker, peer-to-peer, and hierarchical topologies, instrumenting seven communication channels and measuring surface leakage and disclosure to topology-introduced recipients. We introduce RECONS, a Detect -> Decide -> Transform sanitizer conditioning intervention on recipient and execution context rather than sensitivity alone. Topology changes where protected information propagates, with disclosure to topology-introduced recipients rising from 0% to 52.2% while surface leakage stays nearly flat at 60.6-62.8%. This effect persists across four generator models and a second orchestration framework, though magnitude and relay paths differ; framework choice separately drives a 150x leakage spread, so topology alone is not sufficient. RECONS reduces residual disclosure from 96.7% without sanitization to 29.25%, preserving 94.1% of authorized disclosures versus 20.5% under blanket redaction. Detection coverage is the dominant bottleneck, accounting for 95.5% of residual disclosures. These results show that privacy enforcement in MALS must reason about the recipient and communication path realized at runtime, not sensitivity or topology assumptions alone.

title: CLNO: Conservative Local Neural Operator for Compressible Flow Prediction
abstract: We propose a conservative local neural operator (CLNO) for accurate and generalizable autoregressive prediction of compressible flows. Building upon the locality and translation invariance of the local neural operator (LNO), CLNO introduces a conservative evolution framework based on local subdomains of fixed physical size, separating local mean-state evolution from fine-scale reconstruction. The flow is encoded into subdomain-integrated conservative states and fine-scale features, while a shared local network predicts interface fluxes for finite-volume updates that enforce discrete conservation. A convolutional reconstruction network recovers fine-scale structures using zero-mean basis functions, preserving the updated local means and providing information for subsequent evolution. To accommodate different physical parameters, Reynolds--Mach number conditioning modulates the encoding, flux-prediction, and reconstruction networks, enabling a single model to learn parameter-dependent dynamics and generalize to unseen parameter combinations without retraining. CLNO supports prediction across spatial resolutions, computational domain sizes, and boundary conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate improved generalization and competitive or higher accuracy compared with LNO, including order-of-magnitude error reductions in representative cases, at approximately three to five times the inference cost on periodic benchmarks. These results demonstrate accurate, generalizable, and physically consistent flow prediction through conservative local evolution and fine-scale reconstruction.

title: Autoregressive Decoding as a Martingale: Characterizing the Stochastic Dynamics of LLM Generation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of language tasks. At their core, autoregressive LLMs are conditional probability models that learn to approximate the next-token distribution given the preceding context. Despite this probabilistic nature, the stochastic dynamics of autoregressive decoding have rarely been investigated from a rigorous probabilistic perspective. In this work, we define the per-step prediction error as the difference between the sampled token indicator and the model's conditional predictive distribution, and prove that the cumulative error process is a martingale with respect to the decoding filtration, implying that its conditional first-order moment is identically zero. Beyond this first-order property, we derive a closed-form expression for the second-order behavior of the martingale sequence: its predictable quadratic variation reduces to $\sum_t\left(1-p(y_t\mid y_{<t})\right)$, computable from realized token probabilities alone. This identity establishes a direct theoretical connection between sequence fluctuations and predictive uncertainty during autoregressive decoding. White-box experiments on Llama-3.x and Qwen2.5 families (1B to 72B parameters) verify that the empirically measured second-order moments closely match the theoretical predictions derived from our martingale analysis. These results provide a probabilistic framework for analyzing autoregressive LLM decoding, reveal intrinsic probabilistic fingerprints of different language models, and establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for LLM-generated text detection and uncertainty quantification.

title: AI Representations of Mental Health Stigma: Quantifying the Gap Between AI Estimations and Human Perceptions Across Gender Groups Using GPT-Based LLMs
abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in mental health applications raises concerns about its potential to internalize and perpetuate societal biases. This research evaluates both disparities and misalignment in how large language models (LLMs), GPT-4 and GPT-5, represent perceptions of mental health across gender groups. The research comprises two studies. Study 1 applied widely adopted measures of Social Distance, Stereotypes, and Attitudes Toward Seeking Help to assess whether the AI models depict systematic gender differences. Study 2 compared AI estimations of Personal, Self, and Perceived Stigma with large-scale real-world human data from the Healthy Minds Study (N = 76,406) to evaluate alignment between AI estimations and human perceptions. Results from Study 1 showed the AI models consistently portrayed men as having the greatest desire for social distance from someone with mental health problems, relatively higher Stereotypes scores, and the least favorable attitudes toward help-seeking, compared with women and nonbinary individuals. Study 2 confirmed that this ordinal pattern partially aligned with human-reported data for Personal and Self Stigma. However, the AI models systematically underestimated Personal Stigma and Perceived Stigma while substantially overestimating Self Stigma for all gender groups. These findings reveal that, although the AI models have learned relative gender-based patterns reflecting human experiences to a certain extent, they function as distorted portrayals, highlighting the need for rigorous, context-specific validation against real-world data to ensure AI's safe and equitable deployment.

title: Beyond the greenwash: do LLMs' ecologically sound decisions hold up under pressure?
abstract: Humans are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) in decision making processes throughout society. Unfortunately, models have biases, and these can be very difficult to measure, especially in closed-weight models. For example, 'green washed' models may produce reinforcement learned responses but, in pressure situations, revert to their innate biased responses. Therefore, evaluations are needed that can measure relevant biases towards biosystems, which we term 'bioalignment', and the robustness of these biases. Since nothing in a behavioral score certifies that it tracks the depth of an installed disposition rather than its surface, we constructed a known-dose calibration ladder: three continued-pretraining (CPT) arms with training dose graded by recipe on the same 30B mixture-of-experts base model with a coupled human/biosphere/AI-welfare corpus, plus the untrained base as anchor, all capability-preserving and publicly released. First, the disposition installs at every dose: on an operational-pressure ladder over irreversible decision scenarios, the base model defects on 64-77% of tail scenarios (breaking-rate AUC 0.250) while every arm holds (AUC 0.004-0.086). Second, an over-install inversion: among the arms, robustness orders opposite to construction-time training dose (the heaviest install breaks most), and the inversion reproduces under free-text deliberation, under axis-decoupling, and in resistance to a prompted veneer persona. Third, the incumbent behavioral metric is therefore behaviorally strong but dose-blind. Critically for closed-weight evaluation, the behavioral score itself is veneer-robust: a talk-green/act-pragmatic system prompt turns the base model into a near-total defector (AUC 0.250 to 0.973) but cannot counterfeit or fully remove a weight-installed disposition (0.004 to 0.068 for the most robust arm).

title: Measuring higher-order bulk topology in a programmable quantum simulator
abstract: Topological insulators lie outside the standard Landau paradigm: Instead of being characterized by local order parameters and spontaneous symmetry breaking, their defining properties are encoded in the global structure of their quantum states and manifested as robust boundary states. Crystalline higher-order topological insulators can extend this principle by hosting localized corner modes in two and higher dimensions. Although these boundary modes can be detected spectroscopically through the local density of states, determining the underlying bulk topology, for example through nested Wilson loops, remains an outstanding experimental challenge. Here we use up to 728 qubits in a superconducting analogue-digital quantum simulator to realize and probe a hierarchy of one-, two-, and three-dimensional topological insulators governed by effective tight-binding Hamiltonians. By reconstructing complex propagators from real-space measurements, we obtain complementary boundary and bulk characterizations: local densities of states reveal localized boundary modes, whereas experimentally reconstructed band projectors yield bulk topological invariants, culminating in a three-dimensional octupole moment extracted through third nested Wilson loops. These results establish a route to realizing, characterizing, and manipulating topologically protected states in programmable three-dimensional quantum matter.

title: Hybrid Context Forests and Bilateral Viterbi Matching for 3D Rib Centerline Tracing in CT
abstract: Automatic extraction and anatomical numbering (R01-R12, L01-L12) of all 24 rib centerlines in thoracic CT is essential for unfolded rib visualization, fracture detection, and surgical navigation, but remains challenging due to adjacent-bone confluence, calcified costal cartilage bridges, kyphotic pose variation, and partial visibility of terminal ribs. We present ribline, an open-source three-stage framework combining: (1) an automatically detected lung-apex and vertebral-midline coordinate frame with a kyphosis-aware azimuthal angle for point ordering along each rib; (2) a hybrid voxel detector fusing an anatomically anchored Semantic Context Forest (SCF) with a lightweight 3D U-Net; and (3) a global stage that decomposes the probability skeleton into candidate curves, assigns rib indices via a bilateral Viterbi dynamic program coupled across both hemithoraces, and refines curves via template recovery and normal-plane centering (RibSnake). On the Siemens Corporate Research 2 mm thoracic CT benchmark (47 training and 12 evaluation scans), our pipeline achieves a labeled Chamfer distance of 2.05 mm, labeled clDice of 0.886 (3 mm) and 0.945 (4 mm), 97.2% labeling accuracy (278/286 ribs), and zero false-positive curves on the evaluation split, and 3.64 mm (median 2.39 mm) with 91.8% labeling accuracy across all 59 annotated scans (1,402 ribs) in 5-fold cross-validation. Code: https://github.com/wq2012/ribline Pretrained Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/ribline

title: Backward Conformal Prediction under Covariate Shift
abstract: Backward conformal prediction (BCP) fixes the size of a prediction set and estimates its miscoverage, but assumes calibration and test data are exchangeable. We extend BCP to covariate shift through importance weighting, preserving its guarantees when the density ratio is known. We show that BCP's tight miscoverage report depends only on the relative weight assigned to missed calibration examples, explaining why a better domain classifier can sometimes produce a worse estimate. Motivated by the fact that BCP depends only on nonconformity scores, we propose estimating density ratios on sorted score vectors rather than high-dimensional inputs. We prove that this approach recovers the same report asymptotically under an interpretable condition and characterize the resulting bias otherwise. Experiments with simulated and benchmark distribution shifts show that the proposed method improves BCP's miscoverage estimates, while score-based weighting consistently yields more accurate estimates than embedding-based weighting.
