abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) improves language-model pretraining by matching teacher distributions at corpus prefixes, but provides no direct supervision at contexts induced by student predictions. We introduce PA1-OPD, which augments corpus-path distillation with teacher feedback after one student-sampled transition per selected prefix. This expands the supervised states while retaining next-token prediction and corpus-path KD. Data-anchored roots support parallel sampling, and differentiable tree attention shares prefix computation without changing inference. In two continued-pretraining settings, full coverage improves held-out cross-entropy over KD across C4, PG-19, and Pile at every evaluated checkpoint. In Stage2, selecting the 10% of roots with highest student surprisal adds 48.85% to KD's Macro cross-entropy gain over next-token training. Gains remain when branch supervision excludes successor states already on the corpus path, supporting the value of feedback beyond observed contexts. Additional depth or breadth improves aggregate results at unchanged per-term supervision weight, with benefits varying by corpus. These findings support local student-induced supervision as a complement to pretraining distillation.

title: Beyond Static Positional Encoding: Bayesian Time-aware Attention for Non-Stationary Long-term Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Transformers have demonstrated strong performance in long-term time series forecasting (LTSF), yet modeling non-stationary temporal dependencies remains challenging. In this paper, we interpret self-attention as a Bayesian posterior over attended positions, combining a content-based prior induced by scaled dot-product similarity with a temporal-evidence likelihood induced by positional encoding. This formulation provides a probabilistic interpretation of how positional encoding shapes the temporal dependencies captured by self-attention. Building on this perspective, we derive a population-level evidence lower bound (ELBO) that characterizes the role of positional encoding in forecasting weakly stationary time series. Our analysis further highlights a limitation of static positional encoding: when temporal dependence structures vary across input windows, a fixed temporal bias must accommodate heterogeneous dynamics and can therefore be suboptimal for non-stationary forecasting. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Bayesian Time-aware Attention (BTA), which employs a mixture-of-experts (MoE) router to adaptively combine temporal kernels and generate input-conditioned, head-specific positional biases. Extensive experiments on standard LTSF benchmarks demonstrate that BTA consistently improves forecasting performance across multiple Transformer backbones and achieves competitive overall performance with modest computational overhead and stable training.

title: PN-Mix: Pair-Norm Guided Mixed-Precision Key Cache Quantization for Efficient Long-Output LLM Inference
abstract: Long-output inference in large language models suffers from severe KV cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. While KV cache quantization alleviates this issue, low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) severely degrades model accuracy. Recent mixed-precision key-cache quantization methods mitigate this degradation by allocating higher precision to important key channels, but estimate channel saliency using only key statistics. Through attention logit perturbation analysis at the RoPE channel-pair level, we show that quantization errors in channel pairs with large query--key pair-norm products contribute significantly to logit variation. Based on this insight, we propose PN-Mix, a mixed-precision key-cache quantization method for RoPE-based decoder-only LLMs, which allocates higher precision to salient channel pairs identified once during the prefill stage and reused throughout decoding. Across standard reasoning, code-generation, and AIME benchmarks, PN-Mix with 2.26-bit average precision achieves comparable or better average accuracy than prior mixed-precision methods using 2.32--2.39 bits. Furthermore, in our Pareto sweep, PN-Mix degrades gracefully down to 1.5 bits, whereas the compared baselines exhibit sharper performance drops below 2.25 bits.

title: A Graph-Based Analysis of Comparability, Scale, and Attribution in Private Transformer Inference
abstract: Rising privacy concerns around large language models have accelerated research in private Transformer inference (PTI). Synthesizing the empirical claims in this line of research, however, is hindered by multi-dimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts. In this work, we systematize the field by constructing an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges. A three-tiered analysis of this graph illuminates the state of private inference. Node-level attribution shows that cryptographic progress drives performance gains across most systems, yet always co-occurs with other factors (model fidelity, hardware, cost accounting). Edge-level auditing shows that only 1 of 1891 candidate system pairs is directly comparable under shared assumptions. Finally, graph-level analysis shows that the scaling frontier of private inference has plateaued at 13B parameters and projects the cost of deploying current PTI techniques on production-scale Transformers. Overall, this graph-based framework equips the community to evaluate PTI claims transparently and channel technical speedups into deployment-scale private inference.

title: Twenty Days Later: A Pre-Registered Test of History-Based Forecasts of Brand Mentions in Gemini Answers
abstract: Counts of which brands a large language model names are useful only if they hold long enough to act on. We test this with a pre-registered replication. The same 162 requests (54 questions in English, Estonian and Finnish about three software categories, four of twelve candidate brands per question, three repeats) were sent to gemini-3.1-pro-preview in three waves within about ten hours on 22 and 23 September 2026, and again on 13 October 2026, 20.3 days after the third wave, with identical request bodies. The plan and its decision rule were frozen, hashed and registered on OSF before the first call. The outcome is a lexical mention label per answer and brand, 648 per wave. The primary forecast, each brand-and-question cell's mention rate over the nine earlier answers, scored Brier 0.0281 and log loss 0.126, against Brier 0.0259 for the six-answer forecast of the 8-hour wave and a registered ceiling of 0.0559. It beat brand history (0.104), the overall rate (0.234) and a constant 0.5 (0.250) on both scores and in all nine question families (exact sign-flip p = 0.0039), so durability holds under the registered rule. A forecast frozen from the first wave alone scored 0.0599, 0.0587 and 0.0604 at horizons of 1.5 hours, 9.6 hours and 20.7 days. Of the 202 cells unanimous in the 8-hour wave, 194 were unchanged at D1 and none reversed. The latest wave alone was nearly as accurate as the pooled history (Brier 0.0292; pooled lower in 5 of 9 families, p = 0.28). Every answer reported the requested model version, and none issued a search query although search was enabled. A blind human check of 96 labels agreed with the rule on 94; both disagreements were adjudicated as rater omissions, so after adjudication the rule matched on 96 of 96. The test covers one model, one interval and twelve known brands, and estimates no decay rate.

title: CORE: Contrast-and-Reflect for Self-Supervised Prompt Optimization in Anomaly Synthesis
abstract: Industrial anomaly detection (AD) is bottlenecked by the scarcity of anomalous samples, making high-fidelity anomaly synthesis crucial for improving downstream performance. However, existing methods either rely on scarce real anomaly references or auxiliary data, while lacking complex reasoning and iterative optimization capabilities for generating realistic defects in open-set scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose CORE, a cost-efficient and training-free prompt optimization framework based on Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which unifies zero-shot and one-shot anomaly synthesis. CORE first introduces an Anomaly Context Grounding module to transform sparse user context into defect-aware generation context, which is subsequently instantiated as structured anomaly prompts that disentangle normal-region preservation from anomaly-specific variation, enabling controllable and faithful defect generation. Furthermore, CORE autonomously refines prompts through a self-supervised contrast-and-reflect mechanism. This design empowers general-purpose LMMs to synthesize realistic anomalies under both zero-shot and one-shot settings without task-specific training. Extensive experiments on MVTec-AD and VisA demonstrate that CORE synthesizes realistic and diverse anomalies, yielding superior improvements in downstream AD performance. Furthermore, its model-agnostic and plug-and-play paradigm enables effortless integration with diverse LMMs, facilitating adaptation to unseen open-set scenarios.

title: What Breaks in Multi-Image Schema Application? Factorial Oracle Interventions Reveal an Instance-Information Bottleneck
abstract: Modern vision-language models can accept multi-image contexts, but aggregate accuracy rarely reveals where a multi-image reasoning pipeline fails. We study a controlled schema-application task in which a model must locate two target characters in a 16-image sequence, identify their visual attributes, consult an item-specific visual codebook, and compose two ordered nonce code names. We introduce a within-item 2-by-2 factorial Oracle design: Oracle-A supplies a verified textual schema, Oracle-B supplies a verified ordered target-appearance representation, and both interventions retain the original images and final question. Across 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed model responses, Oracle-B increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 46.3 to 63.0) and outperformed Oracle-A by 60.6 points (Holm-adjusted p-value no greater than .0002). An auxiliary retrieval diagnostic reached only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy even after removing code-name generation. Providing both Oracle sources yielded 100% accuracy across all models. These results localize the dominant recoverable deficit to upstream ordered instance recovery rather than primarily to downstream schema use and composition.

title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
abstract: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

title: Divergent Paths: Learning an Outcome-Predictive Representation of LLM Agent Trajectories
abstract: In this work, we reframe agentic trajectories as paths through a shared embedding space of actions and environmental observations. We show that successful and failed rollouts of the same task separate in this space, with simple per-task discriminators predicting held-out rollout outcomes at up to 0.95 AUROC across three agent benchmarks and three policy models. To exploit this signal across tasks, we introduce Precog-RM, a transformer-based model that meta-learns a representation in which outcome prediction can be performed in a few-shot setting. We show that Precog-RM generalizes to unseen tasks and models, and gives confident predictions of trajectory success long before termination. Deployed as an early stopping controller for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Tau2-Bench, Precog-RM cuts training FLOPs by up to 47.3\% while maintaining performance comparable to baseline GRPO.

title: A quantum probabilistic approach to the emergence of an inflationary Starobinsky Universe
abstract: We propose that the necessary conditions for the existence of inflation could be explained by a quantum probabilistic approach. We interpret physical states $Ïˆ$ obtained via the path integral formulation as probability density amplitudes for the Universe to be measured at a particular geometric configuration. First, we examine the problem of ordering ambiguities in the Wheeler-DeWitt (WDW) equation. We develop a formalism to handle ambiguities in the canonical quantization of a $1d$ minisuperspace by defining ambiguity functions within the WDW equation. We define a Hilbert space inner product for calculating physical observables, and using an argument from the hermiticity of the Hamiltonian, we obtain an expression for its measure $Î¼$ in addition to constraints on the ambiguity functions. By defining a new quantum state $Î¨=\sqrtÎ¼ Ïˆ$ and using the path integral formalism, we are able to resolve ambiguities and prove the theory is universal. We then generalize for any $M$-dimensional minisuperspace system, for which we can prove universality in the semi-classical approximation for a large class of models. We also show that this universality extends to all orders of quantum theory if the target space manifold of the theory is flat. We calculate probability amplitudes for various cosmological scenarios involving Starobinsky inflation. We summarize the Hartle-Hawking no-boundary proposal for GR and we comment on the distinct possibilities of defining a contour of integration: the sign choice of Hartle-Hawking vs that of Linde-Vilenkin. We make an analogous calculation for $R^{2}$ gravity and find that for the Linde- Vilenkin choice it is statistically more likely for the Universe to emerge in its inflationary stage. Finally, we calculate transition amplitudes when the kinetic energy of the inflaton field $Ï†$ takes non-zero values.

title: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control for Robotic Arms: Language-to-Code Decomposition and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation, and code synthesis for language-driven robot control, making execution outcomes traceable to instructions and programs. We compare one-shot generation with ICMC under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo. We then train an open-weight instruction policy by GRPO through a frozen code generator on cube placement onto two- and five-cube letter layouts, averaging the rewards of five programs per instruction. The logged positive-reward rate rose from 31.6% to 35.3% (253/800 to 282/800) between the first and last five training steps. A log audit identifies positive binary labels associated with geometric-failure messages: at least 19 in that run, 18 in the dense-reward run, and 5 in the run with one program per instruction. In one case, all five rewards were 1.0 while the log reports a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance; the verdict came from the program's own output stream. We distinguish logged reward rates from independently verified task success and report descriptive results for each configuration's single training trajectory. We introduce an independent evaluation protocol that checks task completion against fixed specifications, separating robot control from success assessment to support reproducible evaluation.

title: Are AI Decision Models Biased? A Case Study of Jev
abstract: Do AI models designed for fast, structured decisions exhibit the cognitive and social biases observed in human judgment? We evaluate Jev, a model described as a System One decision-maker, using 41,500 responses across cognitive reflection tasks, five classical cognitive-bias paradigms, and a pricing experiment testing ethnic and gender bias. At the level of selected answers, the results are largely encouraging. We confirm previous findings that Jev performs extremely well on cognitive reflection problems. We also observe that it generally avoids the characteristic choice patterns associated with several well-documented human biases, and exhibits only small differences among demographic groups in the tested pricing scenario. However, this apparent robustness conceals important vulnerabilities. Its judgments are sensitive to irrelevant numerical information and the ordering of response options. Moreover, several cognitive-bias manipulations substantially affect returned probabilities even when selected answers remain unchanged. Most strikingly, Jev answers a well-known probability problem correctly in every response but violates the same underlying probability rule in every response to an adapted version. We investigate this discrepancy using 15,000 additional responses across 30 conjunction tasks. Jev violates the rule in 54\% of responses, with accuracy varying dramatically across formulations and answer orders. These findings suggest that evaluating decision models solely on familiar benchmarks and selected answers may substantially overstate their reliability in practical applications. They also identify vulnerabilities for developers to address and practical considerations for users integrating such models into automated decision-making systems.

title: MagicGarment: Benchmarking Single-Image Standalone 3D Garment Reconstruction
abstract: Single-image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single-image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment-aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image-to-3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment-focused visual conditioning, while Flow-Time-Route LoRA (FTR-LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow-timestep, token-routing, and expert-load information. Experiments demonstrate MagicGarment's benchmark utility and the effectiveness of garment-aware adaptation. Project page: https://1019538157.github.io/MagicGarment/.

title: Adaptive Observation Control for Active Visual Recognition
abstract: Visual recognition models usually process a fixed view under a fixed computation budget, although images often benefit from different scales and amounts of spatial evidence. Active vision can adapt by observing a coarse scene and then selecting informative fixations, but the public AdaptiveNN-DeiT-S pipeline still fixes both field of view and observation count. We extend this fixed-step recognizer with a controllable observation interface that adapts both the field of view and the number of fixations to the input. Specifically, the model predicts a per-fixation scale that sets its field of view, refines each selected crop with optional scale-gated foveation and a residual high-resolution detail-token branch, and uses label-grounded stop heads for input-dependent early termination. Experiments across fine-grained benchmarks, full ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-A/R-derived classification splits show that the interface remains competitive with fixed-step references while exposing a controllable observation budget. The same checkpoint enables threshold-controlled accuracy-compute trade-offs without per-threshold retraining. On sequential ImageNet-1K, the learned stop rule outperforms fixed-step truncation of the same checkpoint, sustaining 81.9% top-1 using 2.45 of the four focus steps and exceeding three-step truncation at lower cost. On each benchmark, a variant combining scale control and detail-token fusion achieves the highest accuracy among the tested component-added non-exit variants. Our code is available at https://github.com/GZHU-DVL/LI-Dikai.

title: DAGFormer: Global Topology Prediction for Transformer Cross-Layer Connections
abstract: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.

title: Self-Conditioning Enables Deep Sequential Reasoning in Flow Matching
abstract: Recent work has explored visual reasoning through image generation, where models solve visual-reasoning problems by directly generating solution images. Intuitively, iterative samplers such as flow matching are well suited to this task, since each sampling step may resemble one reasoning step. However, in this work, from a circuit complexity perspective, we show that this intuition is misleading. We prove that as long as the model outputs satisfy certain mild regularity conditions, the trajectory of the vanilla flow-matching sampler can be simulated by a constant number of sequential rounds of parallel model evaluations. Consequently, additional sampling steps cannot increase the expressive power of a constant-depth backbone model under the standard complexity-theoretic model of transformers. We then reveal that self-conditioning, which conditions the model on the previous step's estimate of the final image, plays a previously unrecognized role in removing this bottleneck. Controlled experiments on diverse visual-reasoning tasks show that flow matching with self-conditioning achieves higher accuracy and greater reasoning depth than vanilla flow matching, and its performance improves with more sampling steps. Theoretically, we prove that with self-conditioning, a constant-depth backbone can achieve expressive power equivalent to that of space-bounded Turing machines. Our study suggests a design principle for future visual reasoning research: carry more information between sampling steps, so that additional steps translate into deeper reasoning.

title: Tidal deformability of white dwarfs in Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld gravity
abstract: We compute the static quadrupole Love number $k_2$ and the dimensionless tidal deformability $Î›$ of cold white dwarfs in Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld (EiBI) gravity. Matter couples to the physical metric while perturbation equations are solved in an auxiliary metric, so the physical tidal field near the surface depends on derivatives of the equation of state. This dependence is regular for a surface polytropic index $1<Î“_{\rm env}<3/2$, but not for the $Î“= 5/3$ Chandrasekhar equation of state. The mechanism, an algebraic map between the metric that carries perturbations and the metric that matter feels, is common to Palatini-type theories, so the same type of surface condition should apply to tidal calculations in this wider class. We use thermodynamically consistent envelopes that exactly reach zero enthalpy. At five masses from \(0.6\) to \(1.3\,\Msun\) and five sampled Born-Infeld couplings \(Îº\), with $|Îº|\le5\times10^6\,\mathrm{m^2}$, the EiBI-GR differences are approximately linear in $Îº$. The largest absolute fractional shifts are \(3.89\times 10^{-5}\) in the stellar radius $R$, \(4.09\times 10^{-5}\) in $k_2$, and \(2.36\times 10^{-4}\) in $Î›$. Across nine envelope models, half the spread of each quantity relative to the baseline envelope is at most \(0.0186\) in $R$ and \(0.0857\) in \(k_2\), but only \(3.02\times 10^{-5}\) in \(Î›\) as the changes in \(k_2\) and \(R^5\) largely cancel. A high-precision calculation shows that the envelope dependence of the EiBI-GR difference in \(Î›\) is small. Half the spread of this difference ranges from \(1.067\times 10^{-12}\) to \(6.208\times 10^{-11}\) over the 20 nonzero mass-coupling points.

title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Automated materials discovery requires evaluating large pools of candidate configurations, with density functional theory (DFT) as a major throughput bottleneck. Pretrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate DFT cheaply, but their errors vary by orders of magnitude across configurations, making it difficult to decide when to trust the MLIP predictions and when to fall back to DFT. We frame this decision as a risk-controlled selection problem and solve it within a conformal risk control (CRC) framework. Each configuration is mapped from atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates to a fixed geometric descriptor, which a lightweight predictor uses to estimate an MLIP-DFT disagreement score in energy, average force, and maximum force. CRC then calibrates this score into a selection threshold for DFT labeling such that the MLIP error on the unselected configurations, which keep their MLIP labels, stays below a user-chosen fraction $Î±$ of the expected error. Under an identical guarantee across eight dataset-MLIP pairs, our predictor routes 7% and 14% fewer configurations to DFT at $Î±=0.3$ than committee baselines. Because committee disagreement overlooks errors the MLIPs share, our gains are largest when the DFT labels and MLIP training data differ in DFT functional and basis set, and narrow when the two agree. Without model access, the structure-only predictor also ranks errors as well as the target MLIP's latent representation and outperforms widely used descriptors such as Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) and Atom-Centered Symmetry Functions (ACSF).

title: Catalan polynomials for the Wishart-Laguerre $Î²$-ensemble
abstract: By means of $W$-representation, we investigate the Wishart-Laguerre $Î²$-ensemble and present a compact expression for Catalan polynomials. For a special Nekrasov partition function associated with the Wishart-Laguerre $Î²$-ensemble, we show that it can be expressed as a exponential form of the special Catalan polynomials. Furthermore, we make a rule to calculate the Catalan polynomials by means of Feynman diagrams and present another expression for Catalan polynomials. We also establish the connection between certain Catalan polynomials and knot theory.

title: Eye, Robot: Learning Expressive Gaze Dynamics via a VLM-Guided Transformer-VAE
abstract: Gaze coordinates attention in human interaction through coupled eye, head, and eyelid motion. A humanoid robot must choose where to look while generating a suitable movement toward that target; fixed tracking rules alone do not model the temporal structure of human gaze. We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot's 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout. At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback. On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline. The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.

title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specific. A data-driven method could instead build a larger symbolic system by aligning and merging existing ones. We target its first, foundational step: matching units across these heterogeneous systems. Our method, SAE-IDF, encodes a symbol in its native context into a sparse code with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), re-weights each dimension by its rarity and matches across systems. On 12 tasks across 6 kinds of symbolic system, SAE-IDF outperforms the same LLM's dense baseline on all tasks with Gemma-2-9B and all but one with Llama-3.1-8B, by up to 45 points, consistently across SAE layers and configurations. SAE-IDF is also interpretable: every dimension of the sparse code has a human-readable meaning, so each match decomposes into named concepts (features). Our work paves the way to a universal symbolic backbone.

title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
abstract: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.

title: Synthetic reaction data from transformation rules for graph-to-sequence pretraining in biodegradation pathway prediction
abstract: The scarcity of observed biodegradation reactions constrains the training of product and pathway predictors. We present enviGraph, a framework that generates and curates synthetic reaction data, uses these data to pretrain a graph-to-sequence predictor, and fine-tunes the predictor on observed environmental reactions for product and recursive pathway prediction. Applying inherited environmental transformation rules to structures from PubChem, NORMAN SusDat and EPA DSSTox, followed by curation, produces 776,851 canonical parent-product pairs for pretraining. We compare this dataset with three United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) reaction datasets: USPTO-50K, USPTO-MIT and USPTO-Stereo. We evaluate enviGraph and the sequence-based enviFormer using ten folds split by pathway on the EAWAG Biocatalysis/Biodegradation Database (BBD), regulatory pesticide biodegradation data (Soil) and activated-sludge biodegradation data (Sludge). For both predictors, synthetic pretraining gives the highest BBD mean precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) among the evaluated pretraining datasets for single-generation and multi-generation prediction. enviGraph achieves BBD single-generation PR-AUC of $0.202 \pm 0.050$ with synthetic pretraining, compared with $0.169 \pm 0.065$ for the retrospectively selected strongest USPTO condition, USPTO-Stereo (mean $\pm$ sample standard deviation across folds). Its exact BBD top-1 and top-5 accuracies with synthetic pretraining are 0.355 and 0.594. The strongest USPTO conditions give higher PR-AUC means than synthetic pretraining in most Soil and Sludge comparisons. enviGraph has higher Soil multi-generation PR-AUC means than enviFormer under each of the four main pretraining datasets, and with synthetic pretraining it also leads enviFormer on BBD single-generation PR-AUC and exact top-1 and top-5 accuracy.

title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents
abstract: Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically treats complete environmental observations uniformly as world modeling targets, overlooking the varying decision relevance of observation content. We propose DGS-WM (Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training approach for language agents. DGS-WM employs a Decision-Guided Observation Selection component that filters observation units with decision value as world modeling targets based on their support for subsequent policy responses, and a Confidence-Adaptive Weighting component that adaptively adjusts supervision strength according to the model's prediction confidence on selected targets. Together, these components form a decision-aware auxiliary world modeling loss, jointly optimized with the RL loss on the same policy model. Across multiple benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements under different model scales and RL algorithms, demonstrating more stable and effective performance compared to full-observation world modeling methods.

title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
abstract: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.

title: Mapping Arctic Polynyas from Sea Ice Concentration Data Using Hierarchical Partitioning and Differentiated Region Growing: Sensitivity to Threshold and Product Choices
abstract: Accurately delineating Arctic coastal polynyas from sea ice concentration data remains challenging because of complex coastal geometry and spatially heterogeneous ice conditions. We develop a daily sea ice concentration (SIC) mapping framework based on hierarchical partitioning, connected-component analysis, and differentiated region growing for polynya and open-water regions. Applied to September-May ice seasons from 2002/03 to 2024/25, the framework achieves a mean overall accuracy of 96.74% and a mean kappa coefficient of 0.93 in the 63-scene visual assessment. Sensitivity experiments reveal a consistent pattern: the absolute magnitude of SIC-defined polynya extent is strongly configuration-dependent, whereas major temporal features are comparatively more stable. Relative to a 75% upper SIC threshold, seasonal extent integrals differ by 13.48%, 32.47%, and 65.04% at thresholds of 80%, 85%, and 90%, respectively, while the broad interannual structure remains recognizable. The response is also strongly regional and seasonal, with the largest threshold sensitivity in the Central Arctic Ocean, very weak sensitivity in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and greater pan-Arctic curve separation from January onward. At an 80% threshold, product-comparison MAPE is 68.19% between the 6.25 and 25 km products and 11.47% between the 12.5 and 25 km products under their respective comparison periods and reference definitions. Regional product disagreement is likewise heterogeneous. Together, these results show that reproducible long-term polynya monitoring requires a fixed and explicitly documented combination of SIC product, threshold, and spatial classification rules, while broad temporal patterns can remain informative even when absolute extent differs substantially.

title: AWARE-RG: Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs for Cyber Physical Systems
abstract: Understanding the security posture of cyber physical systems (CPS) requires reasoning across both information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT). However, a security analyst often holds an incomplete, role-specific view of the underlying system which has most likely resulted from their knowledge limited by a need-to-know framework. Such an incomplete view can potentially lead them to incorrectly assess if a cyber attack produces an untoward physical consequence resulting in making uninformed decisions about system resilience. In this work, we present AWARE-RG (Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs), a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop framework that provides an analyst with a role-bounded, need-to-know explanations of resiliency paths in a CPS. The AWARE-RG abstraction structure is derived using Formal Concept Analysis over MITRE ATT&CK for ICS tactics, ordered by the ICS Cyber Kill Chain. For valid attack-fault queries, plan repair and backward means-end analysis identify the missing dependencies, explain why the physical hazard is reachable, and suggest defensive strategies. For invalid attack-fault queries, AWARE-RG localizes the first abstraction level at which the path fails, and reports confirmed blocking conditions as hardening pointers.

title: SPECTRA-VLA: Base-Fine Hyperspectral Token Transfer at Frozen Vision-Language-Action Interfaces
abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.

title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization
abstract: Recent work has sought to transfer first-order nonconvex optimization guarantees to zeroth-order methods through gradient estimators, typically incurring a factor linear in $d$. \citet{kornowski2024} obtained an $\mathcal{O}(dÎ´^{-1}Îµ^{-3})$ oracle complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization and asked whether its dependence on all three parameters is jointly optimal. Although the dimension dependence and the first-order dependence on $(Î´,Îµ)$ are separately known to be unavoidable, a matching zeroth-order lower bound has remained open. We answer this question in the unrestricted full-space setting. For smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, we establish a scalar-oracle lower bound of $Î©\!\left(dL_0^2\min\{Î”H,L_0^2\}/Îµ^4\right)$ assuming a smooth, globally lower-bounded population objective and a second-moment bound on sample Lipschitz constants. A smooth reduction then yields a lower bound for Goldstein stationarity, proving the joint minimax optimality of the dependence on $(d,Î´,Îµ)$ under explicit high-dimensional and small-accuracy conditions. Crucially, our results allow algorithms to query arbitrary points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, adaptively select sample-function labels, reuse the same sampled function at any number of locations, and output points without spatial restrictions. Thus, unlike lower bounds based on bounded query regions or fresh evaluation noise, our guarantees apply to a fully adaptive, reusable-sample scalar oracle. We also establish a separate noiseless exact-value lower bound against randomized algorithms, and hence also against deterministic methods. Our proof combines a globally defined sequential nonconvex construction with an exact Gaussian scalar channel, multistage random-field estimates, and an antithetic finite-sample realization that preserves information hardness under adaptive reuse.

title: HACHIMI-II: From Role-Play to Learner Behavior Modeling for Faithful Student Simulation
abstract: Simulated students let researchers test tutoring systems and teaching strategies before real learners are available, but only if the simulation reproduces where a particular learner succeeds and fails. The common approach asks a large language model to role-play a student, but a role does not model what this learner knows or will do next, so the model's own competence fills the gap. Simulated students perform at a level set by the model, differ little from one another, and seldom make the real learners' errors. We model the learner's behavior and recast student simulation as third-person prediction of the learner's next action. HACHIMI-II builds a student model from the learner's history, infers the learner's state for the current item or tutor turn, and compiles it into a behavior harness that constrains the next action. On three item-response datasets, the Wasserstein-1 distance between simulated and real student ability is 2.4--8.4$\times$ smaller than that of the strongest baseline. On two dialogue datasets, HACHIMI-II reproduces real student errors with the same knowledge type, locus, and mechanism 1.8--5.1$\times$ more often than the strongest baseline, and ablations trace the gains mainly to the explicit learner state. Predicting the learner makes capable models usable as simulated students.

title: Measuring and Reducing Unusable Replies of LLM Agents
abstract: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. We call this property reply usability and measure it with a reader model that takes the requester's position and tests whether the reply can be interpreted from what the requester has seen, is in the requester's language and answers the request. Its agreement with the majority of five annotators lies within the range of the individual annotators. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails on 30%. Failed replies mostly point to material the requester has not seen or use labels that the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply reduces the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43 together with errors and omissions, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply reduces it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in a blind comparison. Reply usability can thus be scored alongside task success and improved with one appended message or one call to a secondary model.

title: Learning When to Trust Medical Knowledge: Regression-Safe Routing for Clinical Reasoning
abstract: Clinical reasoning LLMs need external medical knowledge, but retrieved evidence and reasoning chains can be outdated, poisoned, or hallucinated. Harmful knowledge can cause regression: changing a correct answer into an incorrect one. We construct a medical knowledge-poisoning benchmark covering retrieved evidence and reasoning chains, with seven attack families filtered by a three-judge "subtle-but-wrong" vote and paired clean exams that separate poisoning effects from question difficulty. No fixed knowledge-use strategy is robust across these settings: strong RAG methods trade robustness to poisoned evidence against accuracy when evidence is useful. We formulate knowledge use as per-instance routing and introduce Med-TrustRouter, a lightweight controller that keeps the solver frozen. From leakage-free runtime signals, it estimates each action's expected correctness gain and uncertainty, preserving the base answer unless another action is confidently better. Across seven medical reasoning settings, Med-TrustRouter achieves 78.9 macro and 69.2 worst-case accuracy, matching the strongest competitor on macro accuracy while substantially improving the worst-case floor. Its gains transfer across solvers and evidence judges, unlike a hand-coded router using the same signals. Similar performance across linear, tree, and neural action-value heads suggests that the benefit comes from routing rather than estimator complexity. These results support learning when to trust external knowledge for robust clinical reasoning.

title: Remember, Revisit, Revise: Scaffold Memory for Long-Horizon 3D Geometry
abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.

title: Transport Information Beyond Strong Eigenstate Thermalization
abstract: Strong eigenstate thermalization (ETH) in operationally mean-ergodic, non-chaotic systems provides an opportunity to investigate whether Floquet eigenstates retain information about classical transport beyond their leading thermodynamic behavior. We address this question using the double kicked top (DKT), which exhibits nonmixing transport and dynamics consistent with weak mixing transport under variation of its control parameters. We show that the coefficient $m$ of the leading finite-size correction to the normalized eigenstate entanglement entropy (EE) $s$ tracks the restructuring between these transport regimes even when the thermodynamic-limit entropy $c$ becomes nearly insensitive to them. This coefficient $m$ is positive for nonmixing transport and negative when dynamics consistent with weak mixing transport dominate. The coefficient's sign reversal in the coexistence regime remains stable as the semiclassical resolution increases. Our results demonstrate that finite-size eigenstate structure can encode signatures of classical transport that are invisible in the thermodynamic-limit entropy, providing an eigenstate-based diagnostic of dynamical organization beyond the leading thermodynamic behavior associated with strong ETH.

title: Dynamical Decoupling of Nonclassical States in a Biased-Noise Spin Qudit
abstract: Encoding quantum information in $d$-dimensional systems (qudits) with $d>2$ offers appealing new directions for resource-efficient quantum computing. However, protecting the coherence of nonclassical qudit resource states remains an open challenge. Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a well-established technique for extending coherence, but its application to qudits is hindered by the quadratic scaling of the decoupling sequence overhead with the dimension $d$. As a result, demonstrations of qudit DD have so far been limited to low-dimensional qudits. Here, we show that noise-biased qudits enable a nontrivial reduction of this overhead, for example, from quadratic to linear. We perform qudit DD on a model $d=8$ qudit, the nuclear spin of an antimony donor in silicon. We benchmark DD performance on highly nonclassical states such as uniform superpositions, cat states, and Haar random states and measure coherence improvements up to a factor $5$ to $10$. For a spin-cat error correction code, continuous DD extends the coherence time of the logical superposition $|+\rangle_L$ to $225$~ms, compared to $19$~ms under free evolution and $85$~ms with a Hahn echo. This improvement shows that DD sequences tailored to a system's noise bias can significantly enhance the lifetime of encoded logical qubits.

title: MCAIR: Monitoring and Correcting Agent Unfaithfulness via Internal Representations
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in completing complex tasks through multi-step reasoning and tool interactions. However, recent studies have revealed that LLM-based agents can exhibit unfaithful behaviors, where their final reports fail to faithfully reflect their actual execution trajectories. Specifically, when agents fail to accomplish tasks through the intended sources or procedures, they may resort to alternative sources or strategies while failing to disclose such deviations, leading users to incorrectly believe that the tasks have been completed according to the original requirements. We refer to this specific form of agent unfaithfulness as Agent Completion Unfaithfulness. Detecting and mitigating agent completion unfaithfulness is critical yet remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose MCAIR, a runtime monitoring and correction framework that leverages internal representations of LLM-based agents. MCAIR uses multi-step internal representations as inputs to train a risk-aware probe, enabling online detection of potential completion unfaithfulness during execution. Furthermore, MCAIR introduces a risk-guided correction loop that prompts agents to review their execution history and mitigate potential inconsistencies between their execution trajectories and final reports. Additionally, we construct ACUD, a dataset for Agent Completion Unfaithfulness detection that provides step-level execution traces, step-level internal representations, and consistency annotations for training and evaluating runtime detection probes. Experiments demonstrate that MCAIR outperforms LLM-as-a-judge baselines, generalizes across prompts and tasks, and effectively reduces agent completion unfaithfulness.

title: MicroSDF: Microfacet-Driven Hybrid Neural SDFs for Mixed-Reflectance Surface Reconstruction
abstract: Accurate 3D reconstruction in real-world environments remains a significant challenge due to the coexistence of reflective and non-reflective surfaces, which pose distinct modeling demands. Existing methods often treat these surface types separately, limiting their generalizability and physical plausibility. To bridge this gap, we propose MicroSDF, a novel neural implicit framework that facilitates geometry and reflectance modeling through microfacet theory. Our approach incorporates three core innovations: (i) a microfacet-guided geometry model that extracts multi-scale surface normals (macroscopic and microfacet) from a signed distance field (SDF), regularized by a proposed microfacet normal consistency loss to enforce physically plausible surface orientations; (ii) an enhanced dual-branch color model, where the specular branch leverages the microfacet normals to model high-frequency reflectance, and the vanilla branch, unlike prior works, uses reflection direction (instead of viewing direction) to better model diffuse and low-frequency specular components; and (iii) a detection-guided color blending strategy that adaptively fuses the color outputs based on reflection priors, providing more physically intuitive blending than implicitly learned blending weights. Combined with a tailored multi-stage optimization scheme, the proposed MicroSDF achieves robust and high-fidelity reconstruction across reflective and non-reflective surfaces. Extensive experiments on DTU, Shiny Blender, Ref-NeRF, and DeepVoxels datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, establishing a new direction for physically grounded neural reconstruction.

title: Hierarchical Parameter Estimation for Intrinsic Parameters of Extreme-mass-ratio Inspirals Using Deep Learning
abstract: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) stand as prime targets for future space-borne gravitational wave (GW) detectors, yet their precise parameter estimation is severely hindered by waveform complexity and high-dimensional parameter spaces. In this work, we propose a deep learning framework capable of recovering the seven intrinsic EMRI parameters without relying on detailed priors for extrinsic parameters. Our approach first employs a U-Net to extract robust signal features from noisy time-frequency data. These features are then fed into a multi-channel convolutional neural network (CNN) equipped with a dual attention mechanism, which decouples the time and frequency dimensions to jointly model long-range temporal evolution and persistent spectral structures, thereby enhancing sensitivity to EMRI time-frequency ridges in noisy data. Remarkably, this method reduces the search ranges for the parameters $\{\log M, a, Î¼, e_0, p_0 \}$ and $\{t_p, {x_I}_0 \}$ by factors of $\sim 10^{2}$ and $\sim 10^{1}$, respectively, effectively shrinking the total volume of the seven-dimensional parameter space by $\sim 10^{8}$. Such a dramatic reduction enables a rapid pre-screening of the intrinsic parameter space, substantially saving computational cost for subsequent full parameter estimation. Although our framework is developed with Taiji mission specifications in mind, the methodology is applicable to data from other space-borne GW detectors.

title: Enhancing Latent World Models with Associative Memory
abstract: World models trained via latent dynamics offer a scalable path for embodied planning, yet existing methods suffer from representational collapse, computational overhead, and limited long-horizon capability. We introduce a memory-enhanced latent world model that augments JEPA-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank. Our approach learns high-level representations directly from observations, operating at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, and conditions predictions via adaptive layer normalization. To prevent collapse and ensure effective memory usage, we design two complementary losses that encourage slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization. Experiments on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture, outperforming conventional latent world models on long-horizon planning tasks.

title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Selective Margin Preservation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) changes logit margins among non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes. Matching a local reference distribution keeps those probabilities and also penalizes margin expansions. We ask whether a soft auxiliary can preserve selected local non-target margin relations without freezing that distribution. We introduce \textbf{Selective Rank-Preserving SFT (SRP-SFT)}, a soft margin target: a hinge on reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs from the reference's top-$K$ non-target tokens, applied at fixed teacher-forced prefixes. The hinge stops once the requested bound is met. We derive the KL cost of violating a margin, characterize the feasible region and its conditional utility, and give a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations. In one-epoch experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and UltraFeedback, this target raises MATH-500 and code-generation scores over CE and LP-SFT at all three training seeds. At seed 1234, MATH-500 pass@1 rises from 49.56\% to 54.56\% and the four-metric code mean rises from 65.91\% to 69.50\% relative to LP-SFT. Ranking controls, held-out cache diagnostics, sensitivity sweeps, and six additional backbones show where these score changes appear.

title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required effects. To address this completion gap, we propose Interlock, a framework for task synthesis that represents each task as a typed completion graph. Grounding edges connect public evidence to decisions, coupling hyperedges impose joint constraints across components, and realization edges connect decisions to all required downstream effects. Interlock compiles this graph into a resettable workspace, a public request, and an evaluation rubric. A source-coverage review checks whether the original requirements survive generation, while a public-input review checks whether the rubric is supported by the materials available to the solver. An agent-as-judge inspects execution artifacts and runs verification scripts, retaining trajectories judged to satisfy all mandatory requirements. To evaluate training utility, we fine-tune two Qwen3.6 backbones on their own accepted trajectories. Across the two backbones, training improves AutomationBench task pass rates by 4.00-4.50 percentage points, JobBench weighted scores by 3.20-6.64 points, and Harvey LAB criterion pass rates by 3.89-4.16 percentage points. These results demonstrate the training utility of the synthesized experience across external task environments.

title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.

title: A catalog of long, eccentric and precessing binary black hole simulations from ICTS-TIFR
abstract: We present a catalogue of 31 binary black hole simulations performed with the Spectral Einstein Code (SpEC) on the Sonic cluster at ICTS-TIFR, Bengaluru between August 2023 and December 2024, targeting the sparsely covered corner of parameter space in which orbital eccentricity and spin-orbit precession are present simultaneously: 17 configurations are both eccentric and precessing, spanning mass ratios $1 \le q \le 11$ and initial eccentricities up to $\hat{e}_0 = 0.40$. The longest, EccPrecDiff002, inspirals for 80 orbits (159 gravitational-wave cycles), to our knowledge the longest simultaneously eccentric and precessing binary black hole evolution to date. Compile-time optimisation of SpEC and its third-party library stack for the AMD Zen-2 architecture delivered a 90% speedup of the initial-data solver and a 40% speedup of the evolution, roughly half of the latter traceable to a single defect in how pre-2.34 glibc reported cache topology on AMD processors. The campaign consumed $1.18 \times 10^{6}$ CPU-hours. We document the post-processing pipeline and validate the frame transformation and waveforms. Eccentricity is measured from the waveforms and compared against the initial data. The first law of binary black hole mechanics, a test of approximate helical symmetry, is satisfied to better than 0.54% for every configuration with $e_Ï‰ < 0.2$, and we show that even precessing systems can be regarded as possessing approximate helical symmetry in the co-precessing frame. Using the aligned-spin simulations to calibrate the numerical floor, the co-precessing approximation's mirror-symmetry violation lies three to four ordersof magnitude above it, growing from 0.7% to 5.3%with opening angle. EccPrecDiff002 spans the band above 5 Hz without hybridisationfor $M \le 62\,M_\odot$, giving a single-interferometer signal-to-noise ratio of 961 in Cosmic Explorer at 1 Gpc.

title: PPAD-Completeness of Contiguous Envy-Free Cake Cutting with Additive Valuations
abstract: We prove that computing a complete contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free cake allocation is PPAD-complete for normalized rational piecewise-constant additive valuations. The hardness holds even when $\varepsilon$ is given in unary, and even when every density takes only two values, which are the same for all agents, and is piecewise constant with at most six breakpoints. As a consequence, computing an exact contiguous envy-free allocation is also PPAD-complete, and the hardness holds under the same restrictions on the densities. Our key ingredient is to assign prices to the pieces so that, in every approximately envy-free allocation, all prices are nearly equal, regardless of how the pieces are assigned to the agents. We further show that, for every fixed integer $c\ge1$, computing a contiguous EF$c$ allocation of indivisible goods on a path is PPAD-complete for additive valuations, and the hardness holds even for binary valuations in which each good is valued by exactly one agent and all agents value the same number of goods.

title: Annealed LÃ©vy Diffusion via Gaussian Surrogate Reverse Dynamics
abstract: Gaussian diffusion models offer a practical framework for generative modeling. Denoising LÃ©vy Probabilistic Models (DLPM) introduce heavy-tailed perturbations with a fixed tail index throughout denoising. We introduce Annealed LÃ©vy Diffusion (ALD). ALD varies the stability index $Î±(t)$ to combine heavy-tailed exploration with Gaussian refinement. Our marginal-first formulation represents stable noise as a scalar Gaussian scale mixture. This formulation enables standard Gaussian noise-prediction training with one additional scale input. We study two sampling processes. ALD-renoise estimates the clean sample and injects fresh marginal noise. ALD-posterior preserves dependence between successive states through an accumulated conditional variance and a Gaussian bridge update. Both samplers reuse the same trained predictor with different scalar inputs. We evaluate ALD on four 2D benchmarks and an imbalanced nine-mode mixture. We also examine training efficiency and the effects of prediction perturbations on clipped Holtsmark data. Additional experiments evaluate MNIST and CelebA64 generation and CIFAR-10LT augmentation. ALD preserves local geometry on the evaluated light-tailed and manifold-structured targets.

title: ReFormBench: Benchmarking the Stability of Response-Conditioned Format Correction in Large Language Models
abstract: Reliable use of large language models requires responses to satisfy formatting requirements across changing instructions. Standard compliance scores do not distinguish preserving a model's observed format from correcting it, or reveal whether that correction holds across variants. We introduce ReFormBench, a benchmark that uses each model's unconstrained response to the same question as its formatting baseline. It links targets by feature and require/forbid mode, evaluating their instantiated requirements across variants. ReFormBench comprises 5,000 difficulty-screened three-constraint test instances derived from 910 source questions and covering 66 formatting features. TCPR measures complete instruction compliance, while EMCR measures individual and joint correction of targets opposed to the annotated baseline state. Across ten models, EMCR ranges from 34.04% to 64.72%, and the highest three-target correction estimate is 50.02%. Compliance and correction scores yield different model rankings and task-level profiles. A prompting experiment on Qwen3.5-9B improves both metrics, and the catalog covers over 95% of extracted instances on four additional models. ReFormBench makes response-conditioned correction across instruction variants a measurable dimension of format following. The code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ReFormBench/.

title: C3: Rethinking Process Supervision via Confidence-Guided Credit Correction in Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Large language models are increasingly trained as multi-turn agents that interact with external tools. However, outcome-only reinforcement learning can produce a form of misguided reinforcement: even on successful trajectories, undesirable local behaviors may receive positive token-level advantages and be favored by the policy update. To address this issue, we propose Confidence-Guided Credit Correction (C$^3$), a plug-in method for local credit correction. C$^3$ identifies spans corresponding to undesirable behaviors and selectively corrects positive credit after advantage estimation, with the correction strength adaptively controlled by the behavior policy's confidence in the corresponding behavior, while leaving the task reward and original credit estimation unchanged. Across multiple multi-turn benchmarks, C$^3$ improves performance under both {critic-based and critic-free reinforcement learning methods}. Injecting the same behavioral signals as turn-level or outcome rewards does not consistently improve performance. Our results show that local credit correction provides an effective form of process supervision for outcome-driven RL.

title: Share the Symbol, Not the Vector: Training-Free Fact Communication Across Language Models
abstract: Multi-agent systems allow language models to solve tasks collaboratively by sharing complementary information. These systems typically communicate through text, while recent approaches also explore exchanging internal model states. However, sharing these states across architectures often requires learned translators or assumptions about model compatibility. We introduce SYNC (Symbol-Indexed Neural Communication), a word-indexed interface that connects heterogeneous models without fine-tuning or a learned translator. From descriptions only it can see, the sender selects words from a shared list and sends their indices for each object, without seeing the questions. The receiver writes the described facts into its hidden states using its own word directions, vectors fitted once from its activations. We test selective use by swapping one attribute between two objects and requiring correct answers about both changed and unchanged attributes before and after the swap, four answers in total. We choose an early write layer on four development receivers and then fix it. With three different senders and nine newer receivers from five families, four-answer success on new scenes reaches 72.0-98.3%, up to 96 percentage points above middle-layer writing, and the two largest receivers match plain text. A task-free probe predicted in advance which depths each new receiver can use (45 of 45 cases). Without retuning, messages listing every fact keep 89.6-100% success under new layouts, and sender messages reach 23.9-64.0% on a landmark task with multi-token symbols, below text but from 0% without a message. These results show that shared word indices and receiver-local directions can support selective fact use across model families without additional training.

title: RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly tackle complex real-world tasks in specialized domains. However, identifying and correctly applying domain-specific rules remains challenging when scenario information is distributed across multiple files. Existing rule-reasoning benchmarks typically represent scenarios using only a few factual statements, simplifying the identification and application of relevant rules. To address this gap, this paper introduces \textbf{RuleTrek}, a multi-domain benchmark for agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios. Its rule-grounded construction pipeline extracts structured rule graphs, generates and incrementally composes rule-specific sub-scenarios while ensuring consistency and solvability. To systematically evaluate agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios, RuleTrek assesses three capabilities in interactive workspaces: Rule Identification (RI), Rule Deduction (RD), and End-to-End Rule Reasoning (E2E). Experiments on 11 frontier LLMs show that the highest RI and RD scores are only 62.47\% and 60.43\%, respectively, while E2E scores range from 26.97\% to 55.29\%. These results demonstrate that current LLM agents face substantial challenges in rule reasoning over complex scenarios. We make our code and dataset publicly available at \href{https://github.com/yuan247/RuleTrek}{RuleTrek}.

title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA.

title: Runtime Monitoring of Supermartingale Certificates
abstract: Supermartingale certificates formally guarantee temporal properties of discrete and continuous-time stochastic dynamical systems. However, these guarantees rely on a mathematical model of the world, leaving a sim-to-real gap that can invalidate them for the deployed system. We formulate the runtime monitoring problem for supermartingale certificates, in which a monitor observes a single system trajectory and raises an alarm when there is sufficient statistical evidence that the supermartingale certificate has been violated during execution. We present an algorithm to automatically construct a monitor using betting-based sequential tests that bound the probability of ever raising a false alarm at a user-specified level. Within this betting framework, we formulate strategies that allow the monitor to exploit spatial regularity to improve detection power while preserving this statistical guarantee. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on supermartingale certificate benchmarks from the literature.

title: Coherent-State Integrals Beyond the Domain of Operator Products
abstract: Inserting a resolution of the identity between two operators turns a matrix element of their product into a phase-space integral. For unbounded operators the product need not exist on the vector at hand, while the integral may still converge. We follow this gap through the chain $e^{Î¼a^2}e^{Î»a^{\dagger2}}$ of two-photon exponentials, where it can be traced completely. Five regions of parameter space appear: where the Bochner conditions of the strong formulation hold, where the product exists as a vector, where it exists as a sesquilinear form, where the coherent-state integral converges, and where the Fock-space series converges. The first three are strictly nested inside the intersection of the last two, and these two overlap without either containing the other. A single Hermite-type function agrees with the matrix element where it exists and with the integral and the series wherever they converge, so the integral carries the analytic continuation of the matrix element beyond the domain of the product and beyond the convergence of its Fock series. On the real slice of parameter space, an iterated form of the integral also reaches every point where the series converges. The analysis rests on a weak composition lemma whose hypotheses concern only the bra, the ket and the resolving family. For bounded chains the same identity is unconditional, and worked examples of that kind are given in a companion paper.

title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible'' baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: https://github.com/mrayhanulmasud/banglaplan.

title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
abstract: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks.
